name: ATSAMD11D14A-SSUT
title: SAM D11 Arm Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers, 48 MHz, 16 KB Flash, 4 KB SRAM, full-speed USB device, 14 to 24 pins
summary: A small low-power 32-bit microcontroller series on the Arm Cortex-M0+ core at up to 48 MHz, running from one 1.62 V to 3.63 V supply, with 16 KB of in-system programmable Flash and 4 KB of SRAM. It carries a crystal-less full-speed USB 2.0 device, up to three SERCOM serial blocks (USART, SPI, I2C to 3.4 MHz, SMBus/PMBus, LIN slave), two 16-bit TCs and a 24-bit TCC for PWM and motor control, a six-channel DMA controller and event system, a 32-bit RTC, a 12-bit 350 ksps ADC with up to 10 channels, a 10-bit 350 ksps DAC, two comparators and a touch controller for up to 72 channels. ATSAMD11D14A-SSUT is the 20-pin SOIC part with 18 I/O pins, -40 °C to 85 °C, on tape and reel; the series also comes in a 14-pin SOIC, a 20-ball WLCSP and a 24-pin QFN.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M0+ (r0p1), up to 48 MHz, single-cycle multiplier, Micro Trace Buffer
1.62 V to 3.63 V on the single VDDIO/IN/ANA pin; 1.2 V core from the internal regulator
18 GPIOs on the 20-pin SOIC and WLCSP, 22 on the 24-pin QFN, 12 on the 14-pin SOIC
full-speed (12 Mbps) USB 2.0 device, eight endpoints, can run from the internal oscillator
12-bit, 350 ksps, 8 channels on the 20-pin parts (10 QFN, 5 SOIC14), 1/2x to 16x gain, 13 to 16 bits by oversampling
one 10-bit 350 ksps DAC; two analog comparators with window mode
three SERCOMs (two on the 14-pin SOIC): USART, SPI, I2C up to 3.4 MHz, SMBus/PMBus, LIN slave
two 16-bit TCs, one 24-bit TCC with 8 waveform outputs, 32-bit RTC, WDT, SysTick
PTC: 42 mutual-capacitance (7x6) or 13 self-capacitance channels on the 20-pin parts

circuits.title: Power supply connection
circuits.description: One main rail between 1.62 V and 3.63 V feeds the supply input, with a capacitor from that rail to ground. The VDDIO, VDDANA and VDDIN supplies share the single VDDIO/IN/ANA pin, and GND and GNDANA share the single GND pin, both tied to the board ground.

circuits.title: Power supply decoupling
circuits.description: The single supply pin takes the 1.62 V to 3.63 V rail with a 4.7 µF bulk capacitor on the rail and a 100 nF capacitor placed close to the device, both to ground; the GND pin goes to the same ground.

parts.note: close to the device, low ESR

notes: Capacitor values are typical examples.

circuits.title: External analog references, two sources
circuits.description: Two external references feed VREFA (PA03) and VREFB (PA04). Each has a 4.7 µF capacitor at the source and a 100 nF capacitor close to the device, both to ground.
notes: Capacitor values are typical examples. PA03 carries VREFA and PA04 VREFB on the 20-pin SOIC.

circuits.title: External analog reference, one source
circuits.description: One external reference feeds both VREFA (PA03) and VREFB (PA04): a 4.7 µF capacitor at the source and a 100 nF capacitor close to the device at each reference pin, all to ground.
notes: Capacitor values are typical examples.

circuits.title: External reset circuit
circuits.description: RESET (PA28/RST) has a 10 kΩ pull-up to VDD and a 100 nF filter capacitor to ground; a push-button in series with 330 Ω pulls it to ground.
notes: Values are typical examples.

circuits.title: External clock source
circuits.description: An external clock signal drives XIN (PA08); XOUT (PA09) stays unconnected or serves as an ordinary GPIO.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator
circuits.description: A crystal between XIN (PA08) and XOUT (PA09), each side with a 15 pF load capacitor to ground. The crystal goes right next to the device: long lines load the oscillator too much and couple into other circuits.
notes: Load capacitor values are typical examples.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal without load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal straight between XIN32 (PA08) and XOUT32 (PA09), relying on the internal and board capacitance for its load.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal with load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 (PA08) and XOUT32 (PA09) with a 22 pF capacitor from each pin to ground.
notes: Load capacitor values are typical examples.

circuits.title: SWCLK pull-up
circuits.description: A 1 kΩ pull-up from VDD on SWCLK (PA30), which also runs to the debugger.

circuits.title: Cortex debug connector, 10-pin
circuits.description: A 10-pin Cortex debug header: VTref to VDD, two grounds, SWDIO to PA31, SWDCLK to PA30 and RESET to PA28/RST; the remaining four header pins are unconnected.
notes: Header pins: 1 VTref, 2 SWDIO, 3 GND, 4 SWDCLK, 5 GND, 6 to 9 NC, 10 RESET; odd pins in one row, even in the other.

circuits.title: 10-pin JTAGICE3 compatible SWD header
circuits.description: A 10-pin header matching the JTAGICE3 cable: SWDCLK to PA30, SWDIO to PA31, RESET to PA28/RST, VTG to VDD and GND to ground; the other five pins are unconnected.
notes: Header pins: 1 SWDCLK, 2 GND, 3 NC, 4 VTG, 5 SWDIO, 6 RESET, 7 to 10 NC; odd pins in one row, even in the other.

circuits.title: 20-pin IDC JTAG connector
circuits.description: A 20-pin IDC JTAG header, as used by SAM-ICE: VTref to VDD, SWDIO to PA31, SWDCLK to PA30, RESET to PA28/RST, all ten even pins to ground (the four GND* pins may also be left open), the rest unconnected.
notes: Header pins: 1 VTref, 7 SWDIO, 9 SWDCLK, 15 RESET; 4 to 12 GND, 14 to 20 GND*; 2, 3, 5, 11, 13, 17 and 19 NC; odd pins in one row, even in the other.

circuits.title: Low cost USB interface
circuits.description: The USB connector's D+ and D- run as a differential pair to USB_D+ (PA25) and USB_D- (PA24); its VBUS goes out as the VBUS supply, and its GND and shield both go to board ground.

circuits.title: Protected USB interface
circuits.description: As the low-cost USB interface, with a transient protection array and a shield filter. Clamping diodes run from D+ and D- up to VBUS and down to the shield rail, and a fifth clamps VBUS to that rail. The shield rail joins the connector's GND and board ground through 4.5 nF in parallel with 1 MΩ.
notes: The protection parts sit close to the connector.

operation.text: SAM D11 parts share peripherals, a linear address map and hex-compatible code with the rest of the SAM D family, so firmware moves up to larger devices; pins also migrate within the series. The core reaches 2.46 CoreMark/MHz. The PTC senses touch (buttons, sliders, wheels) and proximity by capacitance, on up to 72 channels.

Software picks one of two sleep modes. In idle the CPU halts while other functions may keep running; in standby all clocks and functions halt except the ones configured to stay on. SleepWalking lets a peripheral wake on a condition of its own, such as a crossed threshold or a finished result, so the CPU is woken only when needed. Events, synchronous and asynchronous, still pass between peripherals in standby.

Flash is reprogrammed in the system over the two-pin SWD port, which also serves debugging and trace on chip without disturbing the running code. A bootloader in the part may load new application code over any of the communication interfaces.

An Arm Cortex-M0+ CPU at up to 48 MHz with a single-cycle hardware multiplier and a Micro Trace Buffer; 16 KB of self-programmable Flash and 4 KB of SRAM; up to 22 I/O pins; operation from 1.62 V to 3.63 V; 24-pin QFN, 20-pin SOIC, 20-ball WLCSP and 14-pin SOIC packages.

Six DMA channels and six event-system channels; eight external interrupts plus one NMI; a 32-bit RTC with calendar; a watchdog; a CRC-32 generator. Two 16-bit timer/counters, each usable as 8 or 16 bit, or paired as one 32-bit counter, with compare/capture channels. Each SERCOM can be a full-duplex or single-wire half-duplex USART, I2C up to 3.4 MHz, SMBus/PMBus, SPI or LIN slave. The 12-bit 350 ksps ADC has up to 10 channels, takes single-ended or differential inputs through a 1/2x to 16x gain stage, corrects offset and gain error itself, and oversamples and decimates in hardware to 13, 14, 15 or 16 bits. There is a 10-bit 350 ksps DAC and two analog comparators with a window function.

One 24-bit TCC with up to four compare channels, each with an optional complementary output, for eight waveform outputs. It generates synchronized PWM patterns across port pins, protects deterministically on faults, offers fast decay and programmable dead time between complementary outputs, and dithers to add up to 5 bits of resolution and cut quantization error. Fault, dithering, pattern generation, output matrix, dead-time insertion and swap are all present.

One full-speed (12 Mbps) USB 2.0 interface with the device function and eight endpoints. It needs no crystal: it can run from the internal RC oscillator. DM and DP are on PA24 and PA25, and the 1 kHz start-of-frame output can be routed to PA23.

Every oscillator can drive the system clock: crystal oscillators for 0.4 to 32 MHz and 32.768 kHz, internal 8 MHz, 32.768 kHz and ultra-low-power 32 kHz oscillators, the 48 MHz DFLL and a fractional PLL from 48 to 96 MHz. Clock domains are set independently, so each peripheral can run at its own frequency.
Software identifies the device from DSU.DID.DEVSEL. The least significant byte of the DID reset value holds the die number, the die revision and the device selection.
Every pin is a PORT general-purpose I/O by default. Setting PINCFGn.PMUXEN (n = 0 to 31) gives the pin to a peripheral, and PMUXn.PMUXE/O picks which of functions A to H.

The crystal oscillators are not PORT functions; SYSCTRL registers connect them to PA08 and PA09. Of the debug pins only SWCLK is a PORT function. When a debugger is plugged in, cold or hot, PA31 is switched to SWDIO without software.

VDDIO/IN/ANA supplies the I/O lines, OSC8M, XOSC, the internal regulator, the ADC, AC, DAC and PTC, OSCULP32K, OSC32K and XOSC32K, from 1.62 V to 3.63 V. The regulator makes the 1.2 V that runs the core, memories, peripherals, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M, and holds BOD12. PA02 to PA07 sit beside the analog blocks; PA08 and PA09 beside XOSC. GND is the ground pin.
Normal mode serves the CPU and peripherals running. Low-power mode draws little static current and suits standby.
For the POR to work, VDDIO/IN/ANA must ramp up no slower than a minimum rate and no faster than a maximum rate; the electrical characteristics give both.

The device holds itself in reset after power-up until the supply has settled everywhere. It then starts on 1 MHz: OSC8M divided by eight, fed to generic clock generator 0, which clocks the Power Manager. Some synchronous system clocks run, undivided, at that 1 MHz so code can execute. Of the generic clocks only GCLK_WDT, for the watchdog, is on.
After power-up every I/O pin is left high-impedance.
When reset is released the CPU loads its PC and SP from address 0x00000000, the start of internal Flash. That code then sets up the clock system.

Three monitors. POR watches VDDIO/IN/ANA at all times, including every sleep mode, and resets the whole chip when it falls below threshold. BOD33 watches the 3.3 V supply and is set up in SYSCTRL. BOD12 watches the internal VDDCORE after start-up; it is calibrated in production, its settings sit in the NVM User Row and they must stay unchanged when the user row is rewritten.

High-speed Flash, SRAM read and written in one cycle at full clock speed, and a Flash area set aside for EEPROM emulation. The high-speed bus is a bus matrix with fixed addresses; nothing is remapped, not even at boot.
Read at 0x804000 and loaded automatically at power-on; NVMCTRL writes it. A new value takes effect in the other modules only after the next reset.
Read at 0x806020 and not writable. It holds production-measured calibration values, for the ADC, OSC32K, the USB pads and the DFLL48M, that application code copies into the matching registers itself.

Arm Cortex-M0+ revision r0p1, ARMv6 architecture with the Thumb-2 instruction set; it runs all Cortex-M0 code and its code runs on M3 and M4 cores. It has one 32-bit AHB-Lite system bus to memories and peripherals and one 32-bit single-cycle I/O port to the PORT. The AHB-Lite bus and the I/O port work concurrently, so instruction fetch continues during I/O accesses and single-cycle I/O can be kept up indefinitely.
The System Control Space holds the debug registers. SysTick is a 24-bit timer. The System Control Block reports and controls configuration and system exceptions.
The NVIC takes 32 external interrupts at 4 priority levels, set per interrupt in software. It is tightly coupled to the core for low latency and quick handling of late-arriving interrupts.
A symmetric crossbar switch with a 32-bit data bus, running at the same clock as the masters, letting different masters reach different slaves at the same time.

Each master reaching the SRAM carries its own QoS level. At level 0x00 or 0x01 a RAM access costs at least one cycle of latency. Concurrent accesses are ordered first by QoS level, then by SRAM port ID, the lowest ID first. The MTB is fixed at level 3 and the DSU at level 1. The CPU level is bits [1:0] at 0x41007110, reset 0x0; the USB and DMAC levels are set in their own QOSCTRL registers.

An AHB slave that reaches the peripherals' control registers on the low-power APB side, to APB4: wait states, error reporting, transaction protection and byte, half-word and word transfers, also on reads, with address and data merged into one cycle. CLK_HPBx_AHB must be on for the bridge to work.

One PAC per bridge write-protects the registers of each peripheral on that bridge. At reset the PAC0 and PAC1 bus clocks (CLK_PAC0_APB, CLK_PAC1_APB) run and CLK_PAC2_APB does not; the PAC keeps working in any sleep mode whose clock runs. A debugger ignores the protection. Writing one to a bit of WPCLR lifts protection for that peripheral, writing one to WPSET applies it; both registers read back the same value. A write to a protected peripheral is dropped with an access error (CPU exception). Protecting an already protected peripheral, or unprotecting an unprotected one, also raises an error, which checks program flow; code that changes protection from interrupts should read WPSET first.

The Device Service Unit detects debug probes, lets the Arm Debug Access Port take the debug pads and CPU reset, holds a CoreSight ROM for device identification, and offers memory services (CRC32, MBIST) such as IEC60730 Class B testing needs. It sits on the bus matrix, so debugger and CPU can use it together. Its features: CPU reset extension, cold- and hot-plug probe detection, chip erase, CRC32 over any memory on the bus matrix, two debug communication channels, a DAP security filter and memory built-in self-test. Some are limited while the NVMCTRL security bit is set.

SWCLK belongs to the DSU by default for probe detection and reset extension. Changing its PORT function or disabling its PORT mux turns hot-plugging off until a power or external reset. The DSU runs in any sleep mode whose clock runs; the PM gates its APB and AHB clocks (CLK_DSU_APB, CLK_DSU_AHB). It has no DMA, interrupts, events or analog connections. All writable registers except DCC0 and DCC1 can be write-protected by the PAC; a debugger ignores that protection.

A RESET release with SWCLK held low keeps the CPU in reset, so a debugger can attach before any code runs; STATUSA.CRSTEXT then reads one. Writing one to STATUSA.CRSTEXT lets the CPU run and clears the bit; a written zero has no effect. At start-up SWCLK is pulled up internally, so an unconnected pin is not taken for a debugger. On a device protected by the security bit the CPU cannot be released this way, and the attempt sets STATUSA.PERR.

Cold-plugging finds a debugger while the system is in reset, through the reset extension. Hot-plugging finds one while the system runs, on a falling edge of SWCLK; it cannot work during reset, as POR and RESET reset the detector, and it needs SWCLK left on its debug function (STATUSB.HPE shows whether it is available). Either detection sets STATUSB.DBGPRES. Hot-plugging is unavailable while the security bit is set. Detection needs powered pads, so at cold start it waits for the POR release; on a protected device only cold-plugging can find a probe, so the external reset must outlast the POR, and if reset is released before POR the attempt is repeated until it connects.

Chip erase clears all volatile memory and the Flash array, EEPROM emulation area included, and removes the security bit; the auxiliary rows, user row included, are kept. It starts on a write of one to CTRL.CE, is ignored while the PAC protects the DSU, and is done when STATUSA.DONE reads one. A protected device must be reset by the debugger to be detected. The sequence: cold-plug so the probe is found and the CPU held in reset; write CTRL.CE (volatile memory cleared, Flash array erased, lock row erased); poll STATUSA.DONE; reset so NVMCTRL reloads the fuses.

Programming needs the security bit clear. The debugger holds RESET low at power-up; the regulator keeps the system in POR until the supply passes the POR threshold and the internal supplies settle. The PM starts and switches clocks to the slow clock while the external reset holds the internal resets. With SWCLK held low, releasing RESET cold-plugs the debugger; the debugger then clocks SWCLK and the DAP runs. The CPU stays in reset while the rest of the system starts; a chip erase clears Flash, and programming goes through the AHB-AP. Afterwards the chip restarts on RESET, a power cycle or a write of one to STATUSA.CRSTEXT; SWCLK must be high at RESET release so the CPU is not held again.

Setting the NVMCTRL security bit shuts external tools out of the internal memories until a chip erase. The DSU filters the AHB-AP's transactions: on a protected device an access outside the DSU external range is dropped and answered with an error, raising the AHB-AP sticky error bits. The CPU uses the DSU without limit even when protected. The first 0x100 bytes of DSU registers are the internal range and are mirrored at offset 0x100 as the external range; a protected device lets the DAP make MEM-AP accesses only between offsets 0x100 and 0x2000, and accesses at 0x100 to 0x1FF are then restricted.

A CoreSight ROM table, whose address is in the DAP's MEM-AP BASE register, identifies the vendor and the way to identify the chip, through a 64-bit ID built from PID0 to PID7. The DID register then gives the processor, family, subfamily and device select.

CRC32 and MBIST share ADDR, LENGTH and DATA: set them, then issue the command in CTRL. Any other command is ignored until STATUSA.DONE is set. Enabling the clocks enables the module; its registers can be write-protected by the PAC. A debug adapter uses the external range 0x100 to 0x2000, and on a protected device an access to the first 0x100 bytes returns an error; the CPU uses the internal range 0x0 to 0x100.

The DSU computes a CRC32 over a memory area, Flash or AHB RAM. It uses the standard CRC32 polynomial 0xEDB88320 in reversed form. ADDR takes the word-aligned start and LENGTH the word-aligned size; DATA takes the starting value, normally 0xFFFFFFFF, or an earlier result to chain several blocks. CTRL.CRC starts it and CTRL.SWRST cancels it. When STATUSA.DONE sets, check STATUSA.BERR for a bus error, then read DATA; complement it to match the usual CRC32, or keep it as it is to seed the next run. From the internal range any area can be checked; from the external range on a protected device only the whole Flash array or whole EEPROM area, with the registers forced, which lets a protected part be verified.

DCC0 and DCC1 are two registers with handshake that CPU and debugger can both use, even on a protected device, at run time and in debug mode, for a custom debug protocol. STATUSB.DCC0D and DCC1D set on write and clear on read. On a protected device a debugger cannot attach while the CPU runs. MBIST uses the same registers, so they must stay idle during MBIST.

MBIST runs a March LR test, linear in time (write all 0; bit by bit read 0 write 1, descending; read 1 write 0 read 0 write 1, ascending; read 1 write 0, ascending; read 0 write 1 read 1 write 0, ascending; read all 0, ascending), that finds address decoder, stuck-at, transition, coupling, linked coupling and stuck-open faults; its run time depends on the CPU clock and the number of RAM bytes. It is meant mainly for production test and cannot run from the external range on a protected device (STATUSA.PERR is set). ADDR.ADDR takes the start and LENGTH the size; testing a whole physical memory gives the best coverage. CTRL.MBIST starts it and CTRL.SWRST cancels it. With ADDR.AMOD = 0 (the default) it stops at the first fault or at the end, sets STATUSA.DONE, and sets STATUSA.FAIL on a fault. With ADDR.AMOD = 1 it pauses on a fault with only STATUSA.FAIL set and resumes when one is written to STATUSA.FAIL. On a fault ADDR holds the word address and DATA the failing bit and phase.
An external access is one at DSU offsets 0x200 to 0x1FFF; an internal access is one at offsets 0x0 to 0x100.

Clocks come from three blocks. SYSCTRL owns the sources: XOSC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, OSC8M, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M. GCLK turns a source into clocks for peripherals: each generic clock generator picks a source and can divide it, and each generic clock (the clock input of one peripheral, one per instance where there are several) picks a generator through its multiplexer. Generator 0 is GCLK_MAIN and feeds the Power Manager. Generic clock 0 is the DFLL48M reference when the DFLL multiplies another clock. The PM makes the clocks that run in step with the CPU (CPU, AHB, APB and each peripheral's bus interface), with a mask bit per interface and prescalers for CPU and buses. Example: SERCOM0 run from the open-loop DFLL48M uses generator 1 on DFLL48M, generic clock 20 (GCLK_SERCOM0_CORE) on generator 1, and CLK_SERCOM0_APB unmasked in the PM APBC mask.

Synchronous means the CPU and bus clocks; asynchronous means a clock made by a generic clock. Where a peripheral runs from a different clock than the CPU, register accesses across the two domains are synchronized in hardware, and a SYNCBUSY flag shows when that is under way.

GCLK, WDT, RTC, EIC, TC, ADC, AC and DAC have one synchronizer per peripheral, so only one register in the peripheral is synchronized at a time. Bus-interface (APB) registers need none. Every core register in the generic clock domain is synchronized when written and some also when read; this happens even if both domains run from the same source at the same frequency. A write to a core register sets STATUS.SYNCBUSY until done; while it is set, another core-register write, a read of a read-synchronized register or a read of the register being written stalls the bus. Reading a read-synchronized register stalls the bus straight away without setting SYNCBUSY, and if SYNCBUSY was already set it stalls twice. Completion can be polled, taken from the sync-ready interrupt where one exists, or simply waited out by issuing the next access.

On peripherals with a READREQ register, writing READREQ.RREQ with the register offset in READREQ.ADDR starts a read synchronization and sets SYNCBUSY; when it clears, the value can be read without delay until the next request. READREQ.RCONT keeps that register synchronized continuously so it can always be read without a stall; SYNCBUSY is set only for the first pass. A write to a write-synchronized register stops continuous reading and it must be restarted, and it pauses in sleep modes where the generic clock stops, so a fresh request is needed right after wake-up.

Writing CTRL.ENABLE or CTRL.SWRST also starts a write synchronization and sets SYNCBUSY; ENABLE reads back its new value at once and SWRST reads one until hardware finishes the reset and clears it with SYNCBUSY (writing zero to SWRST does nothing). The sync-ready interrupt cannot signal either. While either is pending, writes to core or APB registers and reads of read-synchronized registers stall the bus; APB registers can still be read.

SERCOM USART, SPI and I2C, I2S, TCC and USB give each write-synchronized core register its own synchronizer and its own SYNCBUSY bit, so different registers can be written back to back. A second write to the same register before its synchronization ends is dropped; writing a 16-bit register as two 8-bit writes discards the second and raises an error, while a 32-bit write updates several registers that may each settle at a different time. Before reading a core register, check that its SYNCBUSY bit is clear: the read itself is immediate but only valid when no synchronization of it is running. ENABLE and SWRST set SYNCBUSY.ENABLE and SYNCBUSY.SWRST.

A peripheral on a generic clock needs a running source, a generic clock generator set to that source and enabled, its generic clock set to that generator and enabled, and its bus interface unmasked in the PM. With the interface masked its registers read as zero and writes are lost.

Every clock source can run on demand: it stays stopped until a peripheral asks for it, the request passing through the generic clock and generator (all of which must be enabled), and stops again once no request is active. Clearing a source's ONDEMAND bit keeps it running regardless, which removes its start-up time at the cost of power. In standby the requests still work for modules set to run in standby (RUNSTDBY).
A slow peripheral clock lowers that peripheral's active power but lengthens synchronization with the CPU domain, so the peripheral responds later and the CPU waits longer.

Any reset: OSC8M on and divided by 8, GCLK_MAIN on OSC8M, CPU and bus clocks undivided. A power reset also leaves every generator off except generator 0 (GCLK_MAIN, OSC8M, no division) and generator 2 (OSCULP32K, no division), and every generic clock off except the WDT's, which runs from generator 2. A user reset restores the same, except for generic clocks locked with WRTLOCK, the WDT clock when the NVM User Row sets WDT always-on at power-up, and the RTC's generic clock when it is enabled. Clock sources return to their reset state on any reset except the 32 kHz sources, which only a power reset resets.

The Generic Clock Controller has eight generic clock generators feeding m generic clock multiplexers, m set by the number of peripherals. A generator takes an internal or external source, optionally divides it, and its output can go to any number of multiplexers; a multiplexer picks one generator to make a peripheral's clock (GCLK_PERIPHERAL), and one generic clock may serve several peripherals. The source of a generator can be changed while running. GCLK runs in every sleep mode if needed; its bus clock CLK_GCLK_APB is set in the PM. It has no DMA, interrupts or events, and has no enable bit of its own.

First the generator's source must be running. Then: one 32-bit write to GENDIV with the generator number in ID and the divider in DIV; one 32-bit write to GENCTRL with the same ID and GENEN set; one 16-bit write to CLKCTRL with the generic clock number in ID and the generator in GEN. CTRL.SWRST resets the GCLK, except generic clocks and their generators that are write-locked.

Each generator can choose among eight sources, generator 1 among seven: generator 1 can be the source of every other generator but not of itself. Generator x pairs with pin GCLK_IO[x], which can be its input (GENCTRL.SRC = GCLKIN) or carry its output. GENCTRL.GENEN turns a generator on; when it reads zero the output is gated off. A change of GENCTRL.SRC from source A to B happens on the fly: the generator keeps running on A until B is ready, holding requests to both, then drops A. GENDIV.DIV divides the source, read in one of two ways set by GENCTRL.DIVSEL; the number of DIV bits differs between generators. An odd division gives an uneven duty cycle unless GENCTRL.IDC is set for 50/50. Generator 0 is GCLK_MAIN for the PM.

operation.topic: Generic clock output on a pin
operation.text: With GENCTRL.OE and GENEN set, the generator requests its source and drives its clock out on GCLK_IO. With OE clear the pin sits at GENCTRL.OOV, low or high, while the generator is off. In standby the pin freezes at OOV unless GENCTRL.RUNSTDBY is set, in which case the clock keeps running out to the pin.

Choose the generator in CLKCTRL.GEN, then set CLKCTRL.CLKEN; CLKEN is synchronized and reads its old value until done, and a disabled generic clock is gated. To change a generic clock's generator without glitches: clear CLKEN, wait until it reads zero, write GEN, set CLKEN again.

Setting CLKCTRL.WRTLOCK locks that generic clock: further CLKCTRL writes are ignored, and the GENCTRL and GENDIV of its generator are locked too. Only a power reset unlocks them; SWRST does not. Generator 0 cannot be locked, being GCLK_MAIN, and any reset returns it to a known set-up.

GENCTRL, GENDIV and CLKCTRL are reached through their ID fields: a write carries the ID of the generator or clock it is for, and to read one, write its ID first (for GENCTRL an 8-bit write to GENCTRL.ID) and then read the register. Which generators and clocks run after reset depends on the device.

In a sleep mode where generic clocks stop, a peripheral that needs its clock asks the GCLK, which wakes the source, then starts the generator and the generic clock in turn and hands the clock over (SleepWalking). In standby the GCLK can keep a generator's output running to GCLK_IO. GENCTRL, GENDIV and CTRL are synchronized when written: STATUS.SYNCBUSY is set at once and cleared when done, and a synchronized access while it is set stalls the bus and the CPU, with interrupts held pending, until it finishes.

The Power Manager handles reset, the synchronous clocks and sleep. From GCLK_MAIN it makes the clocks for the CPU and AHB and for each APB bus, each its own domain whose speed can change at run time, so peripherals can run slower than the CPU; each module's clock can be masked. A clock failure detector can move the main clock to OSC8M. The reset controller gathers every reset source, resets the device and records which source it was. The regulator is in low-power mode during STANDBY, so enough clocks and peripherals must be off before entering it that the regulator is not overloaded.

Power reset sources: POR, BOD12, BOD33. User reset sources: the RESET pin, the watchdog, software reset. Reset cause register. CPU, AHB and APB clock control from GCLK sources with a 1x to 128x prescaler, safe clock switching at run time, per-module clock gating and a clock failure detector. Sleep modes IDLE and STANDBY, with SleepWalking on GCLK clocks.

CLK_PM_APB can be masked in the PM itself; once off, only a reset turns it back on. GCLK_MAIN makes the main clock CLK_MAIN, which feeds one 8-bit prescaler for the CPU, AHB and APB clocks. CLK_CPU drives the CPU; stopping it stops execution. CLK_AHB always equals the CPU clock in phase and frequency but can run while the CPU clock is off, with a gate for each AHB peripheral. Each APBx clock is in step with the CPU clock, can be divided, keeps running when the CPU clock is off, and has a gate for each module on that bus. While the CPU is halted by a debugger the PM keeps working, and in sleep its clocks keep running for the debugger, so power cannot be measured in debug. INTFLAG and RCAUSE are not PAC-protected.

After power-on the PM is enabled, RCAUSE shows POR, the default GCLK_MAIN source is started and calibrated before the CPU runs, CLK_MAIN is GCLK_MAIN undivided and the device is ACTIVE with only the needed clocks on. The PM is always on and cannot be reset. The POR detector holds reset until power is stable, so no external reset circuit is needed for a clean start.

The main clock feeds an 8-bit prescaler; each derived clock runs from any tap or the undivided clock, provided fCPU ≥ fAPBx and no domain exceeds its maximum. CPUSEL.CPUDIV sets the CPU (and AHB) division, APBxSEL.APBxDIV each bus's. All can be rewritten without stopping peripherals, and one write updates all synchronous clocks together, so the CPU can be scaled while APB stays fixed. INTFLAG.CKRDY reads zero from the write until the new setting takes effect, and can raise the PM interrupt when it does; rewriting CPUSEL before CKRDY returns to one can leave the system unstable or hung.

Each AHB or APBx peripheral clock is turned on or off by its bit in the matching mask register; a module on several domains has several bits. With its APB clock off a module's registers cannot be read or written. Turning off the NVMCTRL clock breaks Flash reads by the CPU; turning off the PM's clock or the APB bridge holding the mask registers leaves them unwritable until a system reset.

With CTRL.CFDEN set, the detector watches the undivided main clock and calls it failed if no rising edge arrives within one OSCULP32K period (a failed crystal, say). The main clock then moves to OSC8M, INTFLAG.CFD is set (with an interrupt if enabled) and CTRL.BKUPCLK is set by hardware; writing BKUPCLK to zero selects GCLK_MAIN again but does not cure the fault. It does not watch during start-up after wake-up or in sleep, and must be turned off before standby. It must stay off when the main clock is not much faster than OSCULP32K, as with a 32 kHz RC main clock. OSC8M should be enabled so the switch can happen.

RCAUSE holds the most recent reset cause for the boot code to read. Power resets come from an electrical cause (POR, BOD12, BOD33, all made in SYSCTRL); user resets from the application (the RESET pin, the WDT, and SysResetReq, the CPU's SYSRESETREQ bit in its Reset Control register). RESET resets the device when pulled low; it has an internal pull-up and needs no drive in normal use.

WFI enters sleep; SLEEP.IDLE and the CPU's SCR.SLEEPDEEP pick the mode. IDLE stops the CPU and, by level, some synchronous domains, regardless of the mask registers, with the regulator in normal mode; it wakes fastest. It is entered by WFI with SLEEPDEEP = 0 after setting SLEEP.IDLE, or on leaving the lowest-priority ISR when SCR.SLEEPONEXIT is set, and left on any interrupt the NVIC lets through with enough priority, restarting the CPU and the stopped modules. STANDBY (WFI with SLEEPDEEP = 1, SLEEPONEXIT also available) stops every clock not requested by a running module or set with ONDEMAND = 0 (the RTC, for example, keeps its generic clock), and puts the regulator and RAM in low-power mode. Any peripheral that can raise an asynchronous interrupt wakes it; the CPU then runs the ISR or carries on after WFI, per PRIMASK. In IDLE the PM runs on the main clock; in STANDBY it is frozen until an asynchronous interrupt.

In STANDBY a peripheral can briefly wake the clocks it needs and do its work without waking the CPU, then either wake the device with an interrupt or let it fall back into standby. On this device it works only on GCLK clocks, through on-demand clock sources.

Two interrupt sources: clock ready (CKRDY) and clock failure (CFD). Each has a flag in INTFLAG; a one written to INTENSET enables its interrupt and a one written to INTENCLR disables it, and writing one to the flag clears it.

The System Controller is the interface to the clock sources, the brown-out detectors, the core regulator and the voltage reference: it enables, disables, calibrates and watches them. Their status is gathered in PCLKSR, and changes can raise interrupts through INTENSET, INTENCLR and INTFLAG. BOD33 and BOD12 interrupts can wake the device from standby. It runs in any sleep mode where its source clock runs.

XOSC: 0.4 to 32 MHz crystal oscillator, adjustable gain, programmable start-up, crystal or external clock on XIN. XOSC32K: 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator, automatic or manual gain, programmable start-up, crystal or external clock on XIN32. OSC32K: accurate 32.768 kHz internal oscillator with fine tuning and programmable start-up. OSCULP32K: always-on ultra-low-power 32.768 kHz oscillator, fine tuning, calibration loaded from the factory row at reset. OSC8M: 8 MHz internal oscillator, fast start, fine tuning, 4, 2 and 1 MHz divided outputs, factory calibration loaded at reset. DFLL48M: 48 MHz with no external parts, open loop as a programmable oscillator or closed loop multiplying a known clock. FDPLL96M: 48 to 96 MHz output from a 32 kHz to 2 MHz reference, three reference choices, adjustable PI controller, fractional part giving steps of 1/16 of the reference. BOD33 and BOD12: programmable threshold loaded from the user calibration at start-up, reset or interrupt, continuous or sampled mode with programmable rate, hysteresis. VREF: bandgap with programmable calibration loaded from the factory row, and a temperature sensor. VREG: core voltage trim loaded from the factory row.

SYSCTRL supplies XOSC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, OSC8M, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M to the GCLK. Its bus clock CLK_SYSCTRL_APB is set in the PM. The BOD sampling clock and the DFLL48M control logic (which runs on the DFLL output) are both asynchronous to the bus clock, so writes to some registers are synchronized. While the CPU is halted by a debugger SYSCTRL keeps running. When a debugger is cold-plugged the BOD33 reset is masked; under hot-plugging it stays active. INTFLAG is not PAC-protected.

The chosen reference must be set up and running before the FDPLL96M is used; a GCLK reference must be enabled in the GCLK and lie inside the FDPLL96M input range. XOSC can be divided inside the FDPLL96M, and the divider and crystal must give a reference inside that range. The internal lock timer needs a 32 kHz generic clock (GCLK_DPLL_32K) enabled first.
A 32.768 kHz crystal goes between XIN32 and XOUT32 and a 0.4 to 32 MHz crystal between XIN and XOUT, each with whatever load capacitors it needs.

An oscillator runs only when its ENABLE bit is set. By default it runs in idle only when a peripheral asks (ONDEMAND resets to one) and stops in standby. ONDEMAND = 0 keeps it running in idle. RUNSTDBY = 1 lets it run in standby on request, except the DFLL and DPLL; ONDEMAND = 0 with RUNSTDBY = 1 keeps it always running in standby. OSCULP32K always runs and cannot be turned off. Status signals in PCLKSR can raise interrupts and some can wake the device from standby.

XOSC takes an external clock on XIN or drives a 0.4 to 32 MHz crystal. It is off after reset and XIN/XOUT are ordinary I/O. In crystal mode (XOSC.XTALEN = 1) SYSCTRL takes both pins; in external-clock mode (XTALEN = 0) only XIN, leaving XOUT free as GPIO. XOSC.ENABLE turns it on. In crystal mode XOSC.GAIN must suit the crystal frequency, and XOSC.AMPGC lets the amplitude regulate itself, usually lowering current. After a hard reset or a wake from a mode where it was off it needs time to settle; XOSC.STARTUP sets that time, the output is held off meanwhile, and PCLKSR.XOSCRDY sets (with an interrupt if INTENSET.XOSCRDY) when it ends. Standby must not be entered while an oscillator is starting: wait for its ready bit in PCLKSR.

XOSC32K takes an external clock on XIN32 or drives a 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 and XOUT32. It is off after POR and the pins are ordinary I/O; crystal mode takes both pins, external-clock mode only XIN32. XOSC32K.ENABLE turns it on (XTALEN selects crystal); to turn it off write ENABLE to zero leaving the other bits as they are, since changing ENABLE together with other bits can misbehave. Once on it stays on in every sleep mode. XOSC32K.STARTUP sets the start-up time, during which the output is held off, and PCLKSR.XOSC32KRDY sets when it ends (interrupt with INTENSET.XOSC32KRDY). A 32 kHz crystal can take up to a second to start, so XOSC32K keeps running through every reset except POR. With a crystal it gives a 32.768 kHz output (EN32K) and a 1.024 kHz output (EN1K); neither works with an external clock on XIN32.

OSC32K is a tunable low-power 32.768 kHz RC oscillator, off by default and turned on with OSC32K.ENABLE. EN32K enables its 32.768 kHz output and EN1K its 1.024 kHz output. Its frequency is set by OSC32K.CALIB, which software must write itself from the factory values in the NVM Software Calibration Row; after a CALIB write, wait for PCLKSR.OSC32KRDY before the value takes effect.

OSCULP32K is a tunable ultra-low-power 32.768 kHz oscillator, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature; it suits designs where low power matters more than frequency accuracy. It is on after POR, runs always except during POR, and its 32.768 kHz and 1.024 kHz outputs always run. OSCULP32K.CALIB is loaded from the factory calibration at start-up to correct for process spread and can be overwritten.

OSC8M is an 8 MHz open-loop RC oscillator, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature, the clock used after POR and the backup clock when the main clock fails. OSC8M.ENABLE turns it on and off. OSC8M.CALIB is loaded from the factory calibration at start-up; FRANGE and CALIB can be rewritten to tune the frequency; rewriting them while OSC8M is enabled is not recommended. Being open loop, its frequency moves with voltage, temperature and process. The PM switches it off in some sleep modes.

After any reset the DFLL48M is in open loop, its frequency set by DFLLVAL.COARSE and DFLLVAL.FINE, which may be changed while it runs. Loading the DFLL48M COARSE CAL value from the calibration row into COARSE gives close to 48 MHz. The output is usable once PCLKSR.DFLLRDY sets.

In closed loop the output is held against a reference clock, CLK_DFLL48M_REF, which is generic clock 0. Set-up after enabling: enable the reference; set the largest coarse and fine steps in DFLLMUL.CSTEP and FSTEP (small steps mean little overshoot but slower lock, and neither should exceed half the maximum of COARSE or FINE); set the multiply factor DFLLMUL.MUL, keeping the output under the DFLL maximum (a target under the minimum gives the minimum); then set DFLLCTRL.MODE. COARSE and FINE are then read-only and driven by the tuner, which starts from the COARSE value, so a COARSE near the end value shortens coarse lock. Loading DFLL48M COARSE CAL into COARSE, setting DFLLCTRL.BPLCKC and then starting closed loop cuts the lock time to the fine lock time.

Lock comes in two steps: coarse lock finds COARSE and sets PCLKSR.DFLLLOCKC, fine lock trims FINE and sets PCLKSR.DFLLLOCKF; each can raise an interrupt. The output can be used once DFLLRDY is set, its accuracy depending on which locks are held. In closed loop the ratio between output and reference is measured continually and its difference from MUL is kept in DFLLVAL.DIFF. With DFLLCTRL.STABLE = 0 the tuner follows drift without losing lock, so FINE may change after every measurement. FINE can overflow or underflow when the reference drifts or is unsteady, setting PCLKSR.DFLLOOB; the reference must be stable, an external oscillator is advised and an internal one is not allowed, XOSC32K being the best choice.

If the reference stops or falls below CLK_DFLL48M/(2 × MULMAX), PCLKSR.DFLLRCS sets (interrupt on its rise if enabled); noticing can take around 2^17 output cycles. The DFLL then runs as in open loop and returns to closed loop by itself when the reference comes back.

operation.topic: DFLL48M chill cycle and quick lock
operation.text: A new frequency can take several microseconds to appear at the output, which with a small MUL can upset locking. A chill cycle, in which the output is not measured, is on by default (DFLLCTRL.CCDIS = 1 turns it off) and may double the lock time. Quick Lock, also on by default (DFLLCTRL.QLDIS = 1 turns it off), loosens the lock criteria; it can widen the frequency spread more than chill cycles do, with the same average.

With DFLLCTRL.USBCRM set the DFLL uses the USB start-of-frame, sent every 1 ms by a connected host, as its reference in place of the generic clock; a multiply factor of 0xBB80 gives 48 MHz. In this mode BPLCKC is ignored, the COARSE value is used as the final coarse value (it can be loaded from the NVM OTP row by software) and locking goes straight to the fine search. QLDIS must be cleared and CCDIS should be set for a faster lock. STABLE is ignored and an automatic jitter reduction runs in its place.

operation.topic: DFLL48M wake from sleep and accuracy
operation.text: With DFLLCTRL.LLAW = 0 a DFLL that is turned off keeps its locks and restarts with its old settings even without a reference; once the reference returns, fine tracking corrects any drift if STABLE = 0. With LLAW = 1 it loses its locks and goes through the full lock again. Accuracy at fine lock rests on three things: the fine step size (smaller relative to higher output frequencies), the measurement resolution (a low output-to-reference ratio can lock below target, so a reference of 32 kHz or lower is advised for low target frequencies) and the accuracy of the reference.

The FDPLL96M is a fractional digital PLL: a time-to-digital converter, a digital PI filter, a digitally controlled oscillator and a controller, multiplying a reference by a fractional ratio. The reference CLK_FDPLL96M_REF is CLK_DPLL_REF0 (XOSC32K), CLK_DPLL_REF1 (XOSC, through a divider) or GCLK_DPLL; the output is CK_GATED, gated by the PLL controller, and the internal lock timer needs GCLK_DPLL_32K. With DPLLRATIO.LDRFRAC at zero it works in integer mode, otherwise in fractional mode, which adds jitter. Examples: 32 kHz to 48 MHz is a ratio of 1500, LDR = 1499; 32 kHz to 48.006 MHz is 1500.1875, LDR = 1499 and LDRFRAC = 3. Disabling it resets the output.

DPLLCTRLA.ENABLE turns it on and off; the output is stable once DPLLSTATUS.LOCK is set. A non-zero DPLLCTRLB.LTIME sets a fixed lock time; with LTIME zero the lock follows the PLL status and its time depends on filter and target frequency. DPLLCTRLB.WUF (wake-up fast) opens the output gate at the end of start-up, before the frequency settles, saving several milliseconds. After the first acquisition DPLLCTRLB.LBYPASS decides whether losing lock gates the output. To change reference: disable, change DPLLCTRLB.REFCLK, enable again. DPLLRATIO can be changed while running; LOCK then clears and sets again when the output settles, and INTFLAG.DPLLLCK flags a falling LOCK edge until written one. The PI filter adjusts itself, but DPLLCTRLB.FILTER can override it, and DPLLCTRLB.LPEN bypasses the TDC.

BOD33 watches the 3.3 V VDDANA supply and BOD12 the 1.2 V VDDCORE supply, each in continuous or sampled mode. Threshold, action (reset or interrupt), hysteresis and enable are loaded from the Flash User Row at start-up and POR and can be overwritten in the BOD registers. BOD33 compares VDDANA with BOD33.LEVEL and gives an interrupt or a reset when it falls below; PCLKSR.BOD33DET shows the state. Continuous mode (MODE = 0) is the default for both; BOD12 cannot run continuously in standby. Sampled mode (MODE = 1) turns the detector on briefly at each tick of a clock divided from the 1 kHz OSCULP32K output by PSEL, and off in between. Clear CEN before changing PSEL; in sampled mode wait for PCLKSR.B33SRDY or B12SRDY and then write PSEL. Writes to a BOD register are ignored while its SRDY bit is zero. HYST adds hysteresis in either mode.

The internal regulator makes VDDCORE. It is on after any reset and can be turned off with VREG.ENABLE; its level VREG.LEVEL is loaded from the factory calibration at reset. VREG.VDDMON watches the core supply and forces a power-on reset if it falls below a critical level, letting code run again only once the supply has recovered; that threshold sits well below the BOD12 threshold, so it adds to it.

VREF holds a bandgap reference, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature with VREF.CAL loaded at reset, and a temperature sensor whose output voltage rises linearly with temperature over CMIN to CMAX. VREF.TSEN turns the sensor on and it can be routed to the ADC; VREF.BGOUTEN routes the bandgap to the ADC. VREF.CALIB sets the bandgap level and can be overwritten.

Each sets on a zero-to-one change of the matching PCLKSR bit: XOSCRDY, XOSC32KRDY, OSC32KRDY, OSC8MRDY, DFLLRDY, DFLLOOB, DFLLLOCKF, DFLLLOCKC, DFLLRCS, BOD33RDY, BOD33DET, B33SRDY, BOD12RDY, BOD12DET, B12SRDY. The DPLL adds LOCK (lock asserted), LOCKL (lock fell in normal operation) and LTTO (the LTIME period has passed since start). All share one interrupt line to the NVIC; INTFLAG tells them apart.

DFLL48M control registers can be written only while PCLKSR.DFLLRDY is one; writes at other times are ignored. To read one, write DFLLSYNC.READREQ and read once DFLLRDY is set; reading without the request halts the bus until synchronization ends, except when the DFLL is off. The BOD prescaler counters run apart from the bus too: a write to BOD33 or BOD12 clears PCLKSR.B33SRDY or B12SRDY until synchronized, and meanwhile another write to that register or a read of it stalls the bus. Poll the SRDY bit, use its interrupt, or just issue the next access.

The watchdog resets the system if software does not clear it within its time-out, recovering from runaway or stuck code. An early-warning interrupt can come before the time-out. Window mode adds a closed period at the start in which clearing is also an error, catching code that clears too often. Once enabled it runs in active and every sleep mode from its own clock, independent of the CPU, so it still acts if the main clocks fail. Time-outs run from 8 to 16,000 cycles in normal mode or 16 to 32,000 cycles in window mode, and it has an always-on option.

CLK_WDT_APB is on by default. The WDT runs on GCLK_WDT, set up in the GCLK and asynchronous to the bus clock. It is meant to come from the ultra-low-power oscillator, whose accuracy is low, so the time-out varies between parts and software must allow for that; a more accurate source can be used at higher current. The WDT stops while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless forced to keep running. INTFLAG is not PAC-protected.

CTRL (except ENABLE), CONFIG and EWCTRL can be written only while the WDT is off; writes while it is on or being turned on are dropped, and writes while it is being turned off complete afterwards. Normal mode needs CONFIG.PER; add EWCTRL.EWOFFSET and INTENSET.EW for the early warning. Window mode needs CONFIG.PER, CONFIG.WINDOW and CTRL.WEN, plus the same two for the early warning. At power-on CTRL.ENABLE, ALWAYSON and WEN, CONFIG.WINDOW and PER, and EWCTRL.EWOFFSET are loaded from the NVM User Row. CTRL.ENABLE turns it on and off; it can be turned off only while ALWAYSON is zero.

CONFIG.PER sets one of 12 time-outs from 8 ms to 16 s, and the WDT may be cleared at any point in it. Writing 0xA5 to CLEAR restarts the period; any other value resets the system at once. By default a time-out resets the system and the early warning is off; with INTENSET.EW set, the interrupt comes EWCTRL.EWOFFSET GCLK_WDT cycles into the period. Example: PER = 0x2 and EWOFFSET = 0x1 give the warning at 16 cycles and the reset at 32. An offset beyond the time-out means the reset comes first and no warning is seen.

The period is a closed window (CONFIG.WINDOW, 8 ms to 16 s) followed by an open window (CONFIG.PER, 8 ms to 16 s); the total is their sum. Clearing in the closed window resets the system; clearing in the open window restarts it. The early warning, if enabled, comes at the start of the open window, where a sleeping system can wake, clear the WDT and sleep again.

CTRL.ALWAYSON = 1 keeps the WDT running whatever CTRL.ENABLE says, and only a power-on reset clears it. CONFIG and EWCTRL become read-only, so PER, WINDOW and EWOFFSET are fixed; window mode can still be turned on and off with WEN, and the early warning enabled or disabled.

One source, the early warning, on one interrupt line. CTRL and CLEAR are synchronized when written: STATUS.SYNCBUSY is set at once and cleared when done, INTFLAG.SYNCRDY can signal the end, and a synchronized access while busy stalls the bus and the CPU until done.

The RTC is a 32-bit counter behind a 10-bit prescaler, normally left running to keep time, and can wake the device from sleep on an alarm or compare match, periodically, or on overflow. The lowest-power set-up clocks it from the 1.024 kHz output of OSC32K; the 32.768 kHz output gives finer than 1 ms resolution, and other sources come through the GCLK. From 32.768 kHz the shortest tick is 30.5 µs and time-outs reach 36 hours; with a 1 s tick the longest time-out is over 136 years. Modes: 32-bit counter with one 32-bit compare, 16-bit counter with two 16-bit compares, and clock/calendar (seconds, minutes, hours in 12 or 24 hour form, day, month, year, leap years). It offers digital frequency correction, overflow, compare/alarm and prescaler interrupts and events, and optional clear on match.

It runs in every sleep mode and is reset only by POR or CTRL.SWRST. GCLK_RTC must be set up in the GCLK and is asynchronous to CLK_RTC_APB. Generator 0 must never clock the RTC. It stops while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL says otherwise. INTFLAG, READREQ, STATUS and DBGCTRL are not PAC-protected. A 32.768 kHz crystal with its load capacitors can be fitted on XIN32 and XOUT32.

CTRL.MODE, PRESCALER, MATCHCLR, CLKREP and the EVCTRL register can be written only while the RTC is off. Before enabling, choose the mode, the clock representation and the prescaler. In clock/calendar mode the prescaler must give the counter 1 Hz. CTRL.ENABLE turns it on and off; disable it before CTRL.SWRST, which resets every register except DBGCTRL and leaves it off.

CTRL.MODE = 0. The counter counts up on each rising CLK_RTC_CNT edge to 0xFFFFFFFF, wraps to zero and sets INTFLAG.OVF. COUNT is read and written as 32 bits and compared with COMP0; a match sets INTFLAG.CMP0 on the next counter clock edge. With CTRL.MATCHCLR = 1 the counter clears on the cycle after a match, giving periods longer than the prescaler events allow, and CMP0 and OVF then set together.

CTRL.MODE = 1. The counter counts up to the 16-bit PER value, wraps to zero and sets INTFLAG.OVF. COUNT is 16 bits and is compared with COMP0 and COMP1; a match sets INTFLAG.CMPn on the next counter clock edge.

CTRL.MODE = 2, with a 1 Hz counter clock. CLOCK holds time and date in one 32-bit word: seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 hour by CTRL.CLKREP, changeable only while off), day of month from 1, month from 1 (January) and a year counted from a reference chosen in software. Every year divisible by 4 is taken as a leap year, so the reference must be one, such as 2000. After 23:59:59 on 31 December of year 63 it wraps to 00:00:00 on 1 January of year 0 and sets OVF. CLOCK is compared with ALARM0, the fields compared set by MASK0.SEL; a match sets INTFLAG.ALARM0 on the next counter edge, which with 1 Hz is one second after the match. MATCHCLR clears the counter after an alarm match, setting ALARM0 and OVF together.

Any of prescaler bits 2 to 9 can make an event: with EVCTRL.PEREOn set, an event comes on each rising edge of that bit, PEREO0 every 8 GCLK_RTC cycles, PEREO1 every 16 and so on. These events do not depend on the counter's prescaler setting, except that none are made when CTRL.PRESCALER is zero.

Correction needs CTRL.PRESCALER above 1. Once every 1024 GCLK_RTC cycles a single prescaler count is added or skipped; FREQCORR.VALUE says how many times this is done across 976 such periods, giving steps of about 1 ppm (1.0006 ppm). FREQCORR.SIGN sets the direction: positive speeds the clock up, negative slows it. The correction also stretches or shortens the gap between periodic events when it is applied.

Interrupts: overflow (OVF), compare n (CMPn), alarm n (ALARMn) and synchronization ready (SYNCRDY), on one line. Output events, made like the matching interrupts and each enabled by its EVCTRL bit: OVF, PERn, CMPn, ALARMn. In any sleep mode with its clock running the RTC can wake the device by interrupt, or wake the CPU straight on to the instruction after the sleep if the interrupt controller is not set to take it. Periodic events can also wake the CPU through an event channel with its interrupt enabled.

If its clock runs in shutdown, any RTC interrupt source enabled in INTENSET wakes the device from shutdown. Registers keep their values except INTENCLR/SET (cleared, all interrupts off), READREQ, INTFLAG and DBGCTRL; STATUS shows what happened, including bits set during shutdown. The CPU then starts at the reset address, and software must set up the interrupt controller and re-enable RTC interrupts.

Synchronized on write: CTRL.SWRST, CTRL.ENABLE, COUNT, CLOCK, PER, COMPn, ALARMn, FREQCORR and MASKn. Synchronized on read: COUNT and CLOCK. STATUS.SYNCBUSY is set at once and cleared when done, INTFLAG.SYNCRDY can signal the end, and a synchronized access while busy stalls the bus and CPU until done.

The DMAC holds a DMA engine and a CRC engine. It moves data between memories and peripherals in any direction without the CPU. Each channel takes its own triggers and sends requests to an arbiter, which grants one active channel at a time; the fetch engine loads that channel's transfer descriptor from SRAM before data moves. A higher-priority channel can interrupt a transfer, the running descriptor being written back to SRAM first. Interrupts and events can mark the end of a transfer. Bus interfaces: an AHB master for data, an APB slave for its registers, an AHB master for fetching descriptors and an AHB master for writing them back. The CRC lets software check data for accidental errors.

Six channels, each an independent transfer with automatic descriptor fetch and suspend/resume. Triggers from software, the event system or dedicated peripheral requests. Descriptors in SRAM: single block, or multi-buffer and circular buffer by linking. Four priority levels per channel with fixed or round-robin order inside a level. 1 to 256 kB in one block. Static or incrementing addresses with a configurable step. Interrupts on block complete, error and suspend. Four event inputs and four event outputs, one each for channels 0 to 3: inputs can start normal, periodic or conditional transfers or suspend and resume, outputs can mark the end of a beat, burst, block or transaction. A write-back area per channel holds the running descriptor for error recovery. CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) or CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3) chosen in software.

CLK_DMAC_APB and the AHB clock CLK_DMAC_AHB are set in the PM; the bus clock stays in step with the AHB clock but can be divided and can run while the AHB clock is off. The DMAC runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs, and its interrupts can wake the device. It stops while the CPU is halted by a debugger unless DBGCTRL says otherwise. INTPEND, CHID and CHINTFLAG are not PAC-protected. In standby it is held disabled internally but keeps its settings.

A beat is one bus access, its size set by BTCTRL.BEATSIZE. A burst is one beat on this device and cannot be interrupted. A block is what one descriptor moves, 1 to 64k beats, and can be interrupted between bursts. A transaction is all the blocks of a linked descriptor list. Descriptors must stay in SRAM. A transfer starts on a software, event or peripheral trigger; each beat can give an output event and each block interrupts and an event, and at the end of a transaction the channel is suspended or disabled as configured.

BASEADDR and WRBADDR can be written only with the DMAC off; CTRL.SWRST only with both DMA and CRC off; CHCTRLB (except CMD and LVL) and CHCTRLA.SWRST only with the channel off; CRCCTRL and CRCCHKSUM only with the CRC off. Before enabling: write the descriptor area address to BASEADDR and the write-back area address to WRBADDR, and enable the wanted priority levels in CTRL.LVLENx. Per channel: select it in CHID, set CHCTRLB.TRIGACT and TRIGSRC, and prepare its first descriptor with BTCTRL.BEATSIZE, BTCTRL.VALID, BTCNT, SRCADDR and DSTADDR. For the CRC: CRCCTRL.CRCSRC, CRCPOLY, and CRCBEATSIZE when fed from I/O. CTRL.DMAENABLE, CHCTRLA.ENABLE (after CHID) and CTRL.CRCENABLE turn the parts on. CTRL.SWRST resets all but DBGCTRL; CHCTRLA.SWRST resets a disabled channel.

A channel's first descriptor must be valid before the channel is enabled and triggered. The first descriptors of all channels sit together in channel order from BASEADDR; the descriptors of running blocks are kept together in channel order from WRBADDR. Using the lowest channels saves memory. The two areas can be separate, so a transaction can repeat without rewriting its first descriptor, or the same (BASEADDR = WRBADDR), which saves SRAM and shortens the delay from descriptor fetch to the first burst.

A channel that is enabled and not suspended sends a request on a trigger and joins the pending queue (PENDCH.PENDCHx set). The arbiter picks the next active channel, clearing its pending bit and setting or keeping BUSYCH.BUSYCHx; after its burst the channel rejoins the queue (busy stays set), waits for a trigger, is suspended or is disabled (busy clears). A suspended channel leaves the queue but keeps its pending bit and rejoins on resume; a disabled one leaves and its pending bit clears. ACTIVE.LVLEXx shows levels with work. CHCTRLB.LVL sets one of four levels; with all levels enabled a lower number wins. Inside a level, PRICTRL0.RRLVLENx = 0 gives static order (lowest channel first, which can starve high channels) and 1 gives round-robin, where the last channel served (kept in PRICTRL0.LVLPRIx) goes last next time.

Once granted, the channel's descriptor is fetched from the descriptor area for a new block or the write-back area for one under way, and data moves from source to destination over the data bus. Arbitration runs after every burst; BTCNT drops by the beats in a burst, and on a change of channel the count is written back before the next descriptor is fetched. The optional beat event can fire. When BTCNT reaches zero, VALID is cleared in the internal copy and the whole descriptor is written back; the transfer-complete and suspend interrupts and the block event can fire. If DESCADDR is zero it was the last block and the channel is suspended or disabled per BTCTRL.BLOCKACT; otherwise the next descriptor is fetched and written to the write-back area before arbitration.

Each channel has its own trigger source in CHCTRLB.TRIGSRC. CHCTRLB.TRIGACT chooses what a trigger starts: a block by default, or a beat or a whole transaction. With one descriptor the channel turns off after the block; with a list it turns off after the last descriptor or waits for the next trigger. A trigger during a transfer is kept pending (CHSTATUS.PEND, also in PENDCH); only one can wait and further ones are lost. CHSTATUS.BUSY (and BUSYCH) is set while the action runs.

Source and destination can each be fixed or incrementing. BTCTRL.SRCINC turns on source increment, by one beat, or by 2^STEPSIZE beats when BTCTRL.STEPSEL = 1; BTCTRL.DSTINC turns on destination increment, by 2^STEPSIZE beats when STEPSEL = 0 or one beat when STEPSEL = 1. With increment on, SRCADDR or DSTADDR must hold the address of the last beat of the block, not the first.

A bus error from an AHB slave disables the active channel and sets CHINTFLAG.TERR (with an interrupt if enabled); BTCNT is not decremented and is written back first. Fetching a descriptor with VALID = 0, or resuming onto a next-descriptor address of zero, suspends the channel and sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP and CHSTATUS.FERR.

Several blocks make a transaction by linking: each descriptor's DESCADDR points to the next and the last holds zero. To append, build the new descriptor with DESCADDR = 0 and point the old last one at it. To change a descriptor in a running list: enable the suspend interrupt before starting; build the new descriptor; clear VALID in the one to change; read DESCADDR from the write-back area. If the DMA has not reached it yet, update its DESCADDR, optionally clear its suspend action, set VALID and optionally resume. If the DMA is running it, suspend the channel and wait for the interrupt, update the write-back DESCADDR, clear the flags and resume, then update the list entry the same way. To insert C between A and B: impossible while B runs; if A has not started, clear A's VALID, point A at C and C at B, set A's VALID; if A is running, suspend, do the same, then resume.

Software suspends a channel with the suspend command in CHCTRLB.CMD; it stops after the current burst and the command clears itself. Setting the suspend block action in BTCTRL.BLOCKACT suspends it after that block: it stays enabled and still takes triggers but leaves arbitration. An invalid descriptor (VALID = 0) also suspends it and sets CHSTATUS.FERR. Only an enabled channel can be suspended; disabling clears a pending suspend. Suspension sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP. The resume command restarts a suspended channel where it stopped; given before a suspend, it makes the channel skip that next suspend.

Only channels with event inputs (0 to 3) have these; the event must use a resynchronized path and CHCTRLB.EVIE must be set, the action chosen in CHCTRLB.EVACT. Normal transfer: with TRIGSRC zero, each event triggers a beat or burst; it is taken at once and sets PEND, and an event arriving while pending is lost. Periodic transfer: the event lets a pending peripheral trigger through, for timed protocols or periodic peripheral-to-peripheral moves; PEND sets when both are present. Conditional transfer: each peripheral trigger is stored when an event arrives, setting PEND, for example one peripheral giving the event and another the DMA request. Conditional block: an event must arrive before a block starts and is acknowledged at the end of the block. Suspend: suspends the channel, taken when the current AHB access ends. Resume: resumes it and clears CHINTFLAG.SUSP. Skip next block suspend: resumes a suspended channel, or is held until the next block suspend, which is then skipped.

Channels 0 to 3 can give an event one AHB clock long. CHCTRLB.EVOE enables it and BTCTRL.EVOSEL in each descriptor picks beat, burst or block; for an event at the end of a transaction, select block in the last descriptor only.

Disabling a channel stops it cleanly; disabling the DMAC stops everything. The active channel stops once its current beat completes and the write-back area is updated, so no transfer is corrupted; other channels stop on the next clock. CHCTRLA.ENABLE and CTRL.DMAENABLE read zero once the channel or the whole DMAC is off.

A CRC-n catches any single error burst up to n bits long and all but 2^-n of longer bursts. CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) is the polynomial with terms of degree 16, 12, 5 and 0 (0x1021); CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3) has terms of degree 32, 26, 23, 22, 16, 12, 11, 10, 8, 7, 5, 4, 2, 1 and 0 (0x04C11DB7). CRC-16 is the default. Input comes from a DMA channel or from the APB interface and the result is in CRCCHKSUM; with CRC-32 the value read back is bit-reversed and complemented. It works byte by byte. From a DMA channel it uses the channel's beat size and runs on all data through that channel, ready once the transaction finishes or is aborted; SRAM, Flash or I/O data can be checked by moving it through a channel, with CRCDATAIN as destination. From the APB, set CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE (8, 16 or 32 bits) and have the CPU write CRCDATAIN; a 32-bit word takes 4 cycles, CRCSTATUS.CRCBUSY shows it is working, and new data may be written only when it is clear.

Per channel: transfer complete (TCMPL), transfer error (TERR: a bus error, or an invalid descriptor fetched) and suspend (SUSP), in CHINTFLAG with CHINTENSET and CHINTENCLR; all are ORed into one NVIC line. INTSTATUS shows which channels have an interrupt and INTPEND gives the lowest such channel with its flags. Output event per channel (CH) at the end of a block or beat. Input actions: TRIG (normal or periodic transfer), CTRIG (conditional transfer), CBLOCK (conditional block), SUSPEND, RESUME and SSKIP (skip next block suspend); several may be enabled, and any enabled action follows any connected event.

The External Interrupt Controller turns pins into interrupt lines: 8 external pins (EXTINT[7:0]) plus a non-maskable pin (NMI), each EXTINT with its own interrupt line and mask. Each senses a rising, falling or either edge, or a high or low level, has an optional spike filter, can work asynchronously to wake the device when every clock is stopped, and can give an event. NMI behaves alike but drives the CPU's non-maskable interrupt.

All interrupts work in all sleep modes, though the EIC can mask some to keep the device asleep. CLK_EIC_APB is set in the PM; GCLK_EIC is set up in the GCLK and asynchronous to it. The EXTINT line goes to the NVIC; the NMI line needs no interrupt set-up. Events are pulses. It keeps running while the CPU is halted by a debugger. INTFLAG and NMIFLAG are not PAC-protected.

Order: enable CLK_EIC_APB; enable GCLK_EIC if edges or filtering are used; write EVCTRL, WAKEUP and CONFIGy; set CTRL.ENABLE. With NMI in use, enable GCLK_EIC after writing NMICTRL. CTRL.SWRST resets all registers and leaves the EIC off.

CONFIGy.SENSEx sets each pin's sense (zero is none) and a match sets INTFLAG.EXTINT[x]. After clearing, an edge sense sets the flag again only on a new edge; a level sense sets it at once if the level is still there. CONFIGy.FILTENx turns on a majority filter that samples the pin three times on GCLK_EIC and passes the value two or more samples agree on. Level detection, or detection with the filter off, is made asynchronously without GCLK_EIC; with filtering or edge detection on, the EIC requests GCLK_EIC itself (it must be enabled in the GCLK). Level detection still gives interrupts and events without GCLK_EIC.

The NMI pin senses edges or levels too, set in NMICTRL.NMISENSE, with NMICTRL.NMIFILTEN for the filter. NMISENSE alone enables it; the EIC need not be enabled. After reset it detects nothing. A detection sets NMIFLAG.NMI, which always raises its interrupt.

Interrupts from each EXTINTx (flags in INTFLAG, enabled by INTENSET/INTENCLR) share one line; NMI has its own (NMIFLAG). Each EXTINTx can give an event, enabled by its EVCTRL bit, when its CONFIGy condition is met. In sleep, WAKEUP.WAKEUPEN[x] lets a matching EXTINTx wake the device; setting WAKEUPEN without the matching INTENSET bit is advised against. Only CTRL.SWRST and CTRL.ENABLE are synchronized (on write, with STATUS.SYNCBUSY); no register is synchronized on write or read.

The NVM Controller connects the Flash to the AHB, for reads and writes to every NVM section including calibration and configuration, all memory-mapped, and to the APB, for commands and settings. It has programmable read wait states, 16 separately lockable regions, extra protection for a boot loader, a security bit, power-down of the Flash in sleep through the PM with wake on sleep exit or on first access, and a direct-mapped cache.

It runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs, and the PM puts the Flash in a low-power state on sleep as CTRLB.SLEEPPRM sets. It uses CLK_NVMCTRL_AHB and CLK_NVMCTRL_APB; when the AHB frequency changes the wait states must suit it. It keeps running under a debugger, and the security bit can bar access to the Flash. INTFLAG and STATUS are not PAC-protected. After power-up it runs a start-up sequence during which AHB access waits, and then needs no set-up; it has no enable or reset of its own.

The Flash is made of rows of four pages: a row is the smallest erase, a page the smallest write. A memory-mapped calibration and auxiliary space at NVM base + 0x00800000 holds factory calibration and system configuration and reads like the main array. The lowest rows can be a boot loader section set by the BOOTPROT fuses, protected by BOOTPROT[2:0] and the lock bits of those rows, and the highest rows can be set aside for EEPROM emulation, which can be written whatever the region locks say.

The Flash is split into 16 equal regions, each with a lock bit against write and erase; all are unlocked when shipped. The Lock Region and Unlock Region commands change the region holding the address in ADDR (written by software or left by the last write) until the next reset; LOCK shows the state. The default at reset comes from the user configuration in the auxiliary space, written with the Write Auxiliary Page command and taking effect after the next reset.

Reads and automatic page writes go straight to the main address space over the AHB; erase, manual write and the rest are commands. A command is CTRLA.CMD written together with the key in CTRLA.CMDEX; INTFLAG.READY is low until it finishes and commands given meanwhile are ignored. CTRLB sets power reduction mode, read wait states and write mode. Read data comes after CTRLB.RWS wait states.

A row must be erased before programming, by the debugger Chip Erase for the whole array or the Erase Row command for one row. After programming a region can be locked against stray writes. Data goes first to a buffer holding exactly one page, written in 16- or 32-bit accesses (8-bit writes raise a system exception); each write leaves its address in ADDR and STATUS.LOAD shows the buffer holds data. With MANW = 0 (the default) a page is written automatically once its last word is loaded, and the row must be erased before that last write; a partly filled page needs a manual write. With MANW = 1, load the buffer and then issue Write Page with the key. READY stays low and AHB access waits while programming runs. The buffer returns to all ones after each page write, or by a Page Buffer Clear command.

Erase Row sets every bit of the row holding the address in ADDR (any address in the row) to one; in a locked region it does nothing and sets STATUS.LOCKE. Two commands, one to enter and one to leave power reduction, move the controller and Flash in and out of power reduction, shown by STATUS.PRM.

The user configuration in the auxiliary space sets them. The boot loader occupies the start of the main array and is write-protected. The EEPROM emulation area occupies the top rows and is writable regardless of region locks; the usable EEPROM size depends on the emulation software.

The Set Security Bit (SSB) command locks the whole chip against outside access to protect the code; only a debugger Chip Erase clears it, and PROGE can be checked after the command. The cache is direct-mapped, 8 lines of 64 bits (64 bytes), and cuts power and speeds execution when wait states are needed. CTRLB.CACHEDIS = 0 enables it and CTRLB.READMODE picks one of three modes. The INVALL command in CTRLA empties it, and commands that change NVM contents invalidate the affected lines themselves.

PORT drives the I/O pins, grouped in sets of up to 32. Each pin is general-purpose I/O under software control or is handed to a peripheral. As I/O it is an input or a push-pull output with selectable pull-up or pull-down, drive strength and input sampling, and its input buffer can be turned off to save power. Direction, output value and configuration can be set, cleared or toggled for any pins in one atomic 8-, 16- or 32-bit write without touching the others. PORT sits behind an AHB/APB bridge; DIR, OUT and IN can also be reached over the single-cycle IOBUS.

Pins are named Pxy: x a letter per group of 32 starting at A, y the bit position 00 to 31 (PA24, for example). A pin may offer several peripheral functions; when one is chosen, that peripheral drives the pad and reads its state. Some pins are not present on a given device.

During reset every pin is an input with input buffer, output buffer and pull all off. If PORT is powered down the pad latches keep their output value and pull, but the configuration registers and input synchronizers lose their contents, so PORT must be configured again after power-up. It runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs. CLK_PORT_APB is set in the PM; the CPU main clock serves the IOBUS and the APB clock, divided from it, serves register access through the bridge. IOBUS access beats APB access, which waits on a clash. The input synchronizers run on the CPU main clock. PORT keeps running under a debugger. Choosing an analog function for a pin turns off its digital features.

The IOBUS is a single-cycle path from the CPU straight to PORT, without wait states, taking byte, halfword and word accesses at 0x60000000 with the same register layout. Over it, DIR and OUT accept reads, writes, sets, clears and toggles, and IN can be read. Since it cannot wait for IN to resynchronize, CTRL must enable continuous sampling of every pin read this way, or stale values come back.

A DIR bit set to one makes the pin an output and its OUT bit drives it high or low; zero makes it an input. PINCFG holds further settings. IN reads the pin through a synchronizer whether it is input or output, unless PINCFGy.INEN is zero. Setting PINCFGy.PMUXEN and the selection in PMUXn hands the pin to a peripheral line instead of PORT. After reset, standard pins are on PORT with outputs off and input buffers off, even with no clocks; pins with special roles such as the debugger's may differ.

Pin y's register set starts at PORT + (y / 32) × 0x80 and the pin is bit y % 32 in it. DIRSET and DIRCLR, OUTSET, OUTCLR and OUTTGL change single bits without disturbing other pins. An input can be read from IN once PINCFGy.INEN is set. By default the synchronizer only runs on a read, which adds two CLK_PORT cycles; writing the SAMPLINGn field of CTRL (n = (y % 32) / 8) keeps a group of eight pins sampled all the time, at higher current. PINCFGy is at byte offset PINCFG0 + (y % 32). The peripheral selection is at byte offset PMUX0 + (y % 32) / 2, bits 3:0 for even y and bits 7:4 for odd y; the chosen peripheral must also be set up and enabled.

PINCFGy sets push-pull, open-drain or pull, and because pull lives there no unwanted intermediate states appear while direction or value change. With pull enabled, OUT chooses pull-up (1) or pull-down (0). A push-pull output drives the pin to its OUT level, limited only by the pin's own drive; turning the output driver on turns pull off. An input with no external pull floats.

The Event System links peripherals directly, with low delay and no CPU, bus or RAM load. Generators send events, users act on them; a peripheral can be both. Six channels, each connectable to any generator, with an asynchronous, synchronous or resynchronized path and an edge detector; 18 generators and 44 users; each user picks the channel it listens to; software events; SleepWalking and interrupts for low-power use.

Events can wake the CPU from every sleep mode even with the channel clock and bus clock off. In sleep, a channel on the synchronous or resynchronized path restarts its generic clock GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNELx just long enough to handle an event and lets it stop again, without waking the system (SleepWalking); the asynchronous path needs no clock. A software reset returns all registers to reset values and cancels events under way. CLK_EVSYS_APB is set in the PM and each channel's generic clock must be enabled in the GCLK before use. It keeps running under a debugger. INTFLAG is not PAC-protected.

Set up the generator and user peripherals first. Then the user, always before the channel: one 16-bit write to USER with the channel in USER.CHANNEL and the user in USER.USER. Then the channel: one 32-bit write to CHANNEL with CHANNEL.CHANNEL, PATH, EDGSEL and EVGEN. To read back a user, write USER.USER with an 8-bit write and read USER as 16 bits; for a channel, write CHANNEL.CHANNEL with an 8-bit write and read CHANNEL. Channels start connected to no generator (EVGEN = 0x00). The EVSYS is always on; CTRL.SWRST resets it and cancels events.

Asynchronous: the event goes straight from generator to user, even with the channel clock off; no interrupts, status or edge detection (the user handles edges); the lowest delay when generator and user share a generic clock. Synchronous: for a generator on the same generic clock as the channel, otherwise changes can be missed. Resynchronized: for a generator on a different clock; the channel resynchronizes the event.
