Both of these give interrupts and CHSTATUS bits, and with CTRL.GCLKREQ = 0 request their clock only when an event passes (SleepWalking); GCLKREQ = 1 keeps it on.

The synchronous and resynchronized paths need edge detection, chosen in CHANNEL.EDGSEL: rising, falling or both. A pulse generator cannot use both; pick the edge that suits its idle level. CHSTATUS.CHBUSYx is set while an event on channel x is not yet handled by every user; CHSTATUS.USRRDYx is set when every user on it is ready.

Writing CHANNEL.SWEVT with CHANNEL.CHANNEL makes an event on that channel, useful for debugging and acting like any generator. It needs a synchronous or resynchronized path (PATH = 0x0 or 0x1), rising edge (EDGSEL = 0x1) and CTRL.GCLKREQ = 1.

Per channel, on one shared line: overrun (INTFLAG.OVRx), set when a user on the channel is not ready for a new event or a new event comes before the last was handled by all users; and event detected (INTFLAG.EVDx), set when the channel's generator event is seen. Neither works on the asynchronous path. The EVSYS can wake the device from any sleep mode with an interrupt.

A SERCOM is one serial engine that is set up as a USART, an SPI or an I2C interface; once a mode is chosen and the SERCOM enabled, all of it serves that mode. The engine holds a transmitter with one write buffer and a shift register, a receiver with a shift register feeding a two-level receive buffer, a baud-rate generator and address match logic (used by SPI and I2C). It runs from its generic clock or from an external clock, so it can work in every sleep mode, and it can be served by the DMA. I2C mode is SMBus compatible.
A SERCOM has four internal pads, PAD[3:0]. The mode's signals are routed onto them by a multiplexer set from that mode's registers, and the pads reach the pins through PORT.

The bus clock CLK_SERCOMx_APB is on after reset and is switched in the Power Manager. Two generic clocks serve it: GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE, needed for master operation, and GCLK_SERCOMx_SLOW, needed only by some functions. Both are set up and enabled in GCLK before use. They are asynchronous to the bus clock, so writes to some registers need synchronization.

The SERCOM can run in any sleep mode and its interrupts can wake the device. Its DMA request lines go to the DMAC and its single interrupt line to the NVIC; it has no events. In debug halt it keeps running unless set to halt. Every writable register can be write-protected by the PAC except INTFLAG, ADDR and DATA; protection is lifted while the CPU is halted in debug. It has no analog connections.
Register fields are synchronous to the system clock; the shift registers, the receive buffer and the baud-rate generator can run on GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE or an external clock.
CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 enables the SERCOM and 0 disables it. CTRLA.SWRST = 1 returns every register except DBGCTRL to its reset value and disables the SERCOM.

The generator divides the baud reference fREF (the serial engine clock, internal or external) by the BAUD value. Asynchronous operation transmits from the divide-by-16 output and receives from the divide-by-1 output; synchronous operation uses the divide-by-2 output. The selection follows the operating mode. Asynchronous arithmetic mode uses a 16-bit BAUD value (0 to 65,535). Asynchronous fractional mode uses a 13-bit BAUD value, which must be at least 1, and a 3-bit fractional part FP; it is the mode used for auto-baud. Synchronous mode uses an 8-bit BAUD value (0 to 255). S, the samples per bit, is 16, 8 or 3.

The arithmetic-mode formula gives the average fBAUD over 65,536 fREF cycles. Over one frame, only BAUD values that add a whole serial-engine cycle per frame change the average rate, so many neighbouring BAUD values give the same frame timing.

The address logic matches on seven or eight bits, depending on mode, in one of three ways. Address with mask: ADDR.ADDR is compared with the received address, ignoring bits set in ADDR.ADDRMASK; a mask of all zeros matches one address and all ones matches every address. Two addresses: a match on either ADDR.ADDR or ADDR.ADDRMASK. Range: any address from ADDR.ADDRMASK (lower limit) up to ADDR.ADDR (upper limit), both included.

Interrupt sources depend on the mode. Each has a flag in INTFLAG, set when its condition occurs, and is enabled in INTENSET and disabled in INTENCLR; the request stays active until the flag is cleared, the interrupt disabled or the SERCOM reset. All sources share one interrupt line, so INTFLAG tells which fired. Interrupts must also be enabled in the NVIC. DMA requests are defined per mode; the SERCOM has no events.

The SERCOM works in any sleep mode in which its serial clock (external, or from the baud-rate generator) runs, and its interrupts can wake the device. Because the bus clock and GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE are asynchronous, a register may need synchronization on write, on read, on both, or not at all. During it STATUS.SYNCBUSY is set and clears when done; a Synchronization Ready interrupt can signal the end. Starting another synchronized access while SYNCBUSY is set stalls the bus: the access completes, but the CPU waits and interrupts stay pending meanwhile.

The USART mode of a SERCOM: full duplex, asynchronous with clock recovery or synchronous, on an internal or external clock. Frames have 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 data bits, 1 or 2 stop bits, odd, even or no parity, LSB or MSB first. It detects buffer overflow and frame errors, filters noise (false start-bit detection and a digital low-pass filter) and detects collisions. With an internal clock it runs up to half the system clock, with an external clock up to the system clock. It offers RTS/CTS flow control, IrDA modulation and demodulation up to 115.2 kbps, LIN slave support with auto-baud and break detection, start-of-frame detection, DMA, and works in all sleep modes. The write buffer lets frames follow each other with no gap.

The USART runs in any sleep mode where its clock source runs; its interrupts wake the device. CLK_SERCOMx_APB is switched in the Power Manager; GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must be set up in GCLK before use and is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes need synchronization. DMA requests go to the DMAC, the interrupt line to the NVIC; there are no events and no analog connections. In debug halt it keeps running unless DBGCTRL halts it. Every writable register can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA; protection does not apply to an external debugger.

A frame is one start bit (always low), 5 to 9 data bits LSB or MSB first, an optional odd or even parity bit placed after the data and before the first stop bit, and one or two stop bits (always high). A new frame can follow at once, or the line returns to idle, which is high. RxD receives, TxD transmits and XCK carries the clock in synchronous mode.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN and TXEN) and BAUD can be written only while the USART is disabled; writes while it is enabled or being enabled are dropped, and writes during disabling take effect once disabled. Before enabling: choose external or internal clock (CTRLA.MODE 0x0 or 0x1); asynchronous or synchronous (CTRLA.CMODE); the receive pad (CTRLA.RXPO); the transmit and clock pads (CTRLA.TXPO); character size (CTRLB.CHSIZE); bit order (CTRLA.DORD); for parity, CTRLB.PMODE and CTRLA.FORM = 0x1; stop bits (CTRLB.SBMODE); with an internal clock, BAUD; then enable the receiver and transmitter with CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN. CTRLA.ENABLE enables, CTRLA.SWRST resets every register but DBGCTRL and disables.

In both modes the shift clock comes from the baud-rate generator or from the XCK pin. CTRLA.CMODE = 1 is synchronous, 0 asynchronous; CTRLA.MODE = 0x1 picks the internal clock and 0x0 the external one. Asynchronous mode uses the full 16-bit BAUD value, synchronous mode its eight low bits.

In synchronous mode CTRLA.MODE sets XCK as output or input. RxD is sampled on the XCK edge opposite to the one that changes TxD. With CTRLA.CPOL = 0 data changes on the rising XCK edge and is sampled on the falling edge; with CPOL = 1 it changes on the falling edge and is sampled on the rising edge. When XCK is an input (MODE = 0x0) the shift registers run straight from it, unsynchronized to the system clock, so XCK can run up to the system frequency.
Transmit and receive data share one address, DATA: a write goes to the transmit register, a read returns the receive register.

Writing DATA starts a transmission; the data moves to the shift register once it is empty and a whole frame is sent. Write DATA only while INTFLAG.DRE is set. INTFLAG.TXC is set when the frame and its stop bits are out and no new data waits. Clearing CTRLB.TXEN disables the transmitter only after the shift register and the transmit register are empty.

Reception starts on a valid start bit; bits are sampled at the baud rate or XCK and shifted in up to the first stop bit, then the frame moves to the two-level receive buffer and INTFLAG.RXC is set. A second stop bit is ignored. Read DATA only while RXC is set. Clearing CTRLB.RXEN flushes the receive buffer and loses any frame in progress.

STATUS holds three error bits: FERR for a frame error, BUFOVF for an overflowed buffer and PERR for a parity error. Each stays set until a one is written to it, and all clear when the receiver is disabled. With CTRLA.IBON = 1, BUFOVF is set at the moment of overflow and software can drain the receive FIFO by reading until RXC clears. With IBON = 0 the overflow travels through the FIFO with the data and BUFOVF is set with RXC once that data is read.

Clock recovery aligns incoming frames to the internal baud clock; data recovery samples each bit and low-pass filters it for noise immunity. How much mismatch is tolerated is set by how accurate the internal baud clock is, by the incoming rate and by the frame length.

The receiver tolerates only a limited difference between the incoming bit rate and its own baud rate; outside it frames cannot be aligned to the start bit. Mismatch comes from reference clock instability and from the baud divider not reaching the exact rate; pick the BAUD value with the smallest error. The recommended receiver error limits assume the transmitter and receiver share the total error equally.

CTRLA.FORM = 0x1 adds a parity bit. With CTRLB.PMODE = 0 (even) the parity bit is one when the count of ones in the data is odd, so the total is even; with PMODE = 1 (odd) it is one when the count is even. On reception the computed parity is compared with the received bit and STATUS.PERR is set on a mismatch.

RTS and CTS give out-of-band flow control, wired TXD to the remote RXD, RXD to its TXD, CTS to its RTS and RTS to its CTS. It needs the internal clock (CTRLA.MODE = 1), asynchronous mode (CTRLA.CMODE = 0) and CTRLA.TXPO = 2, the pinout with flow control. RTS is driven high while disabled or while the receive FIFO is full, telling the remote to stop after its current frame; RXEN changes RTS after a synchronization delay, and a full FIFO sets RTS at once while the frame in progress waits in the shift register. STATUS.CTS shows the CTS level; a character starts only while CTS is low, and when CTS goes high the transmitter stops after the current frame.

IrDA-compliant modulation up to 115.2 kb/s needs CTRLB.ENC = 1, asynchronous mode (CTRLA.CMODE = 0) and 16x sampling (CTRLA.SAMPR[0] = 0). Each low bit is sent as a high pulse 3/16 of a bit period wide. The decoder synchronizes on each zero pulse and accepts a pulse at least as long as RXPL.RXPL sets; the bit is handed on at the middle of the bit time. With RXPL.RXPL = 19 a pulse must last at least 20 serial-engine clock cycles, which at BAUD = 0xE666 (160 cycles per bit) is 2/16 of a bit. Transmit and receive polarity are opposite: a zero is sent as a high pulse and an accepted pulse is received as a zero.

Available with an auto-baud frame format (CTRLA.FORM = 0x04 or 0x05), asynchronous mode and 16x sampling with fractional baud generation (CTRLA.SAMPR = 1). It follows LIN: a frame starts with a break field and a sync field. More than 11 consecutive dominant bits at the set baud rate is a break; INTFLAG.RXBRK is set and the next character is expected to be 0x55. If it is not, STATUS.ISF and INTFLAG.ERROR are set and the baud rate is kept. Otherwise a counter runs over the 8 bit times of the sync field; its 13 upper bits (count divided by 8) become BAUD.BAUD and its 3 lower bits BAUD.FP, loaded after a synchronization delay. Data characters follow.

With the transmitter and receiver joined, by pin configuration or outside, CTRLB.COLDEN turns on collision detection; RXEN and TXEN must both be set. Each transmitted bit is compared with the received bit; reception while the transmitter is idle is not a collision. On a collision the transfer is aborted, the transmit buffer flushed and the transmitter disabled (CTRLB.TXEN = 0, SYNCBUSY.CTRLB set until done, TxD tri-stated); STATUS.COLL and INTFLAG.ERROR are set, and INTFLAG.TXC is set since the buffer is empty. Software re-enables the transmitter once SYNCBUSY.CTRLB is clear.
Setting CTRLA.RXPO and CTRLA.TXPO to the same pad loops transmit to receive; the loop runs through the pad, so the pin carries the signal as well.

With CTRLB.SFDE = 1 a falling edge on RxD powers up the 8 MHz internal oscillator and starts the USART clock, so the rest of the frame can be received if the baud rate is slow enough against the oscillator start-up time, which varies with supply and temperature. In standby, GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must come from that fast-start oscillator. It works in asynchronous and synchronous modes. With INTENSET.RXS set, the Receive Start interrupt fires at the start bit; without it the oscillator and USART clock stay on through the frame but the CPU wakes only on Receive Complete, if enabled.

In asynchronous mode each bit is decided by a majority vote of three samples in its middle, chosen by CTRLA.SAMPA. With SAMPA = 0 these are samples 7, 8 and 9 at 16x oversampling and samples 3, 4 and 5 at 8x.

DMA requests: RX, set while the receive FIFO holds data and cleared by reading DATA; TX, set while the transmit buffer is empty and cleared by writing DATA. Interrupt sources: Error, Received Break, Clear to Send Input Change, Receive Start, Receive Complete, Transmit Complete and Data Register Empty, each with an INTFLAG bit, enabled in INTENSET and disabled in INTENCLR, all on one line. There are no events.

With the internal clock, CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1 keeps GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE running in every sleep mode and any interrupt can wake the device. With an external clock, RUNSTDBY = 1 lets Receive Start or Receive Complete wake it. With RUNSTDBY = 0 the internal clock stops when the current transfer ends and Receive Start or Transfer Complete can wake the device; an external clock is disconnected after the current transfer and all reception is dropped.

A synchronized write sets its SYNCBUSY bit at once and clears it when done; another synchronized access while the bit is set gives a peripheral bus error. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST (SYNCBUSY.SWRST), CTRLA.ENABLE (SYNCBUSY.ENABLE), CTRLB.RXEN and CTRLB.TXEN (SYNCBUSY.CTRLB).

The SPI mode of a SERCOM: full duplex on four wires (MOSI, MISO, SCK and SS), single-buffered for transmit and double-buffered for receive, in all four SPI modes, LSB or MSB first, with 8- or 9-bit characters and DMA. Running in one data direction frees the MISO or MOSI pin for another use. As master it clocks up to 12 MHz from the 8-bit baud generator and can drive SS in hardware. As slave it accepts a clock up to the system clock, offers optional 8-bit address match, works in all sleep modes and can wake on an SS transition.

The SPI runs in any sleep mode and its interrupts wake the device. CLK_SERCOMx_APB is switched in the Power Manager; GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE must be set up in GCLK before use and is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes need synchronization. DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC; no events, no analog connections. In debug halt it keeps running unless DBGCTRL halts it. Every writable register can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS and DATA; protection does not apply to an external debugger.

The master starts a transaction by pulling the slave's SS low, generates SCK, and ends it by pulling SS high. Data goes master to slave on MOSI and slave to master on MISO; for every character shifted out one is shifted in. A transaction holds one or more characters of 8 or 9 bits. While a character is being sent the next can be loaded into DATA, and each received character moves into the two-level receive buffer.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except RXEN), BAUD and ADDR can be written only while the SPI is disabled; writes while enabled are dropped and writes during disabling complete afterwards. Before enabling: CTRLA.MODE = 0x2 (slave) or 0x3 (master); CTRLA.CPOL and CPHA for the transfer mode; CTRLA.FORM for the frame format; CTRLA.DIPO for the receive pad; CTRLA.DOPO for the transmit, SS and SCK pads; CTRLB.CHSIZE; CTRLA.DORD; in master mode BAUD, and CTRLB.MSSEN = 1 for hardware SS; then CTRLB.RXEN to enable the receiver. CTRLA.ENABLE enables and CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables.
As master (CTRLA.MODE = 0x3) SCK comes from the baud-rate generator in synchronous mode using the 8-bit BAUD value. As slave (MODE = 0x2) the external SCK clocks the shift register directly.
Transmit and receive data share the DATA address: a write loads the transmit register, a read returns the receive register.

With CTRLB.MSSEN = 0 SS can be any GPIO set as output, and software pulls it low before and high after the transaction; with MSSEN = 1 hardware drives it. A character written to DATA moves to the shift register when that is empty, which sets INTFLAG.DRE so the next can be written. With the receiver enabled each received character moves to the receive buffer in the clock cycle of its last bit and sets INTFLAG.RXC. INTFLAG.TXC is set when the last character is out and DATA holds nothing new.

While SS is high the slave is idle with MISO tri-stated; DATA may be written whenever INTFLAG.DRE is set. With SS low and SCK running it shifts according to the transfer mode; DRE sets when DATA moves to the shift register and RXC when a character is received. SS going high ends the transaction and sets INTFLAG.TXC. A value written to DATA needs as many as three SCK cycles before it is ready to load, and it loads at the next character boundary, so the first character of a transaction is not DATA unless preloading is used. For several characters in one transaction, write DATA while at least three SCK cycles of the current character remain, or the previous received character is sent. DRE sets three CLK_SERCOM_APB cycles after DATA empties.

STATUS.BUFOVF is the one receive error; it stays set until a one is written to it and clears when the receiver is disabled. With CTRLA.IBON = 1 it is set at the moment of overflow and software can read DATA until RXC clears. With IBON = 0 it travels with the data and is set, with INTFLAG.ERROR and RXC, when that data is read; the data then reads zero.

In slave mode with CTRLA.FORM = 0x2 the first character of a transaction is checked against the address logic. On a match INTFLAG.RXC is set, MISO is enabled and the transaction is handled; otherwise the whole transaction is ignored. A match can wake the device from sleep. With 9-bit characters only the lower 8 bits are compared with ADDR.

At the start of a transaction the slave first sends what is in its shift register: the reset value after a reset or the last character of the previous transaction. With CTRLB.PLOADEN = 1 one character written to DATA while the synchronized SS is high is preloaded into the shift register, removing the dummy character; a second write before SS goes low waits in DATA. Allow enough time from SS low to the first SCK sampling edge for SS to synchronize to the system domain plus the MISO-to-SCK setup time.

With MSSEN = 0 the master can drive one GPIO SS per slave, slaves in parallel sharing MOSI, MISO and SCK, and only the selected slave drives the shared tri-state MISO. Alternatively slaves can be chained in series on one common SS, hardware or software driven; the master then shifts n characters for n slaves.
Setting CTRLA.DIPO and CTRLA.DOPO to the same data pad loops the data through the pad, so it also appears on the pin.

In master mode with CTRLB.MSSEN = 1 hardware drives one SS: low for at least one baud cycle before transmission and at least one after, and high for at least one baud cycle between back-to-back frames. The gap T between SS and SCK edges is one to two baud cycles depending on the transfer mode. With MSSEN = 0 software drives SS by GPIO.
In slave mode with CTRLB.SSDE = 1 a falling edge on SS sets INTFLAG.SSL and can wake the device.

DMA requests: RX, set while the receive FIFO holds data and cleared by reading DATA; TX, set while the transmit buffer is empty and cleared by writing DATA. Interrupt sources: Error, Slave Select Low, Receive Complete, Transmit Complete and Data Register Empty, each with an INTFLAG bit, enabled through INTENSET and INTENCLR, on one shared line. There are no events.

As master the generic clock keeps running in idle; with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1 it also runs in standby, and any interrupt can wake the device. With RUNSTDBY = 0 GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE stops when the current transaction ends. As slave, RUNSTDBY = 1 lets Receive Complete wake the device; with RUNSTDBY = 0 all reception, including the current transaction, is dropped.

A synchronized write sets its SYNCBUSY bit and clears it when done; another synchronized access meanwhile gives a peripheral bus error. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST (SYNCBUSY.SWRST), CTRLA.ENABLE (SYNCBUSY.ENABLE) and CTRLB.RXEN (SYNCBUSY.CTRLB), RXEN with its own behaviour described under CTRLB.

The I2C mode of a SERCOM, master or slave, compatible with Philips I2C, SMBus and PMBus, with DMA. It supports 100 kHz, 400 kHz, 1 MHz and 3.4 MHz at low system clock frequencies. The pads have slew-rate limited outputs and filtered inputs. As slave it works in all sleep modes, wakes on address match and matches in hardware 7-bit and 10-bit addresses: a unique address and/or the 7-bit general call, an address range, or two unique addresses (usable with DMA). The master uses the baud-rate generator; the slave uses the address match logic.

The I2C runs in any sleep mode where its clock source runs, and its interrupts wake the device. CLK_SERCOMx_APB is on after reset and switched in the Power Manager. GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE is needed for master operation and GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW for some functions (the SMBus time-outs); both are set up in GCLK before use and are asynchronous to the bus clock. DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC; no events, no analog connections. In debug halt it keeps running unless DBGCTRL halts it. Every writable register can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS, ADDR and DATA; protection does not apply to an external debugger.

SDA carries data and SCL the clock. The master sends a start condition, a 7-bit address and a read/write bit; the addressed slave acknowledges, then 9-bit packets follow, 8 data bits and an acknowledge bit. After a NACK from either side the master either sends a stop condition or a repeated start.

CTRLA (except ENABLE and SWRST), CTRLB (except ACKACT and CMD), BAUD and, in slave operation, ADDR can be written only while the interface is disabled. Before enabling: CTRLA.MODE = 0x4 (slave) or 0x5 (master); optionally CTRLA.LOWTOUT for an SCL low time-out, in master mode the inactive bus time-out (CTRLA.INACTOUT), the SDA hold time (CTRLA.SDAHOLD) and smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN); in slave mode the address mode (CTRLB.AMODE) and ADDR.ADDR and ADDR.ADDRMASK; in master mode BAUD. CTRLA.ENABLE enables; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables.

Start and stop detectors and a bit counter watch the bus in all sleep modes while the master is enabled; STATUS.BUSSTATE reads the state: UNKNOWN (0b00) after enabling, IDLE (0b01), OWNER (0b10) and BUSY (0b11). From UNKNOWN the state goes to IDLE when software writes BUSSTATE, on a stop condition, or on an inactive bus time-out; it never returns to UNKNOWN. A start by another master makes the bus BUSY until a stop (or an SMBus inactive time-out). Writing ADDR.ADDR in IDLE issues a start and enters OWNER; a stop command returns to IDLE, and a lost arbitration moves to BUSY until a stop. A repeated start changes the state only if arbitration is lost during it.

In Standard, Fast and Fast-mode Plus the SCL low and high times come from BAUD, while rise and fall times come from the bus. Because of the wired-AND bus the fall time counts as part of the low time, and the rise time lasts until a high level is seen. The low period, the stop setup time, the bus free time, the start hold time and the repeated-start setup time are all timed with the SCL low count, BAUD.BAUDLOW when non-zero or BAUD.BAUD when BAUDLOW is zero; the high time uses BAUD.BAUD. TFALL can usually be taken as zero. Fast-mode Plus calls for a nominal SCL high:low ratio of 1:2. At least one of BAUD.BAUD and BAUD.BAUDLOW has to be other than zero.

The master is byte oriented and interrupt driven, handling most events itself; smart mode (CTRLA.SMEN) cuts software work further. With CTRLA.SCLSM = 0 SCL is held before or after the acknowledge bit; with SCLSM = 1 interrupts come only after the ACK bit, for use when DATA need not be checked before acknowledging. SCLSM = 1 is required for High-speed mode.

A transaction starts when software writes the slave address and the direction bit into ADDR.ADDR; on a busy bus the master waits for idle, then sends a start and the address. Then one of four cases. Arbitration lost or bus error: INTFLAG.MB and STATUS.ARBLOST set (plus STATUS.BUSERR for a bus error), SDA output off and SCL released; the master may not act until the bus is idle, and all flags clear at the next ADDR.ADDR write. No ACK: INTFLAG.MB and STATUS.RXNACK set, clock held; send a stop or a repeated start. Write with ACK: INTFLAG.MB set, RXNACK cleared, clock held; write DATA to send, write ADDR for a repeated start, or stop. Read with ACK: the first byte is received, INTFLAG.SB set, RXNACK cleared, clock held; acknowledge and continue (done by reading DATA in smart mode), send a new address, or stop, with smart mode sending ACK or NACK per CTRLB.ACKACT. STATUS.RXNACK always holds the last acknowledge received. Under SMBus the slave must ACK its address.

After a write address is acknowledged the master sends each byte written to DATA, watching for collisions; INTFLAG.MB is set whether or not arbitration was lost, with STATUS.ARBLOST telling which, and RXNACK must be checked before each next byte; after a NACK no more bytes may be sent. Receiving with SCLSM = 0: when SB is set one byte is in and the master must answer ACK or NACK; if arbitration is lost while sending a NACK, MB is set instead of SB. With SCLSM = 1: when SB is set the byte is in and ACKACT has been sent; set ACKACT for the next byte, then read DATA and, outside smart mode, issue a command.

A master code 0000 1nnn is sent in full-speed mode by writing it to ADDR with ADDR.HS = 0; no slave acknowledges it, and arbitration happens only in this phase. On the master write interrupt, writing the slave address with ADDR.HS = 1 sends a repeated start and the address in High-speed mode, which lasts until a stop. Each repeated start in High-speed mode needs ADDR.HS = 1 again. The master must be set to High-speed (SPEED = 0b10) with SCLSM = 1.

With TENBITEN = 1 a write to ADDR sends two address bytes (11110 addr[9:8] W, then addr[7:0]); the transaction always starts with the read/write bit ADDR.ADDR[0] = 0. A NACK on the first byte raises the write interrupt with the NACK bit; otherwise the write interrupt comes after the second byte. For a read: write ADDR.ADDR[10:1] with TENBITEN = 1 and ADDR.ADDR[0] = 0; on the master write interrupt write ADDR[7:0] as 11110 addr[9:8] 1 with TENBITEN cleared, which sends a repeated start; then transfer data.

The slave is byte oriented and interrupt driven, with smart mode (CTRLA.SMEN). With CTRLA.SCLSM = 0 SCL is held before or after the acknowledge; with SCLSM = 1 interrupts come only after the ACK bit: for a master read the address and data interrupts come together after the address acknowledge, and for a master write the first data interrupt follows the first byte and its acknowledge. SCLSM = 1 is required for High-speed mode.

After a start the address is checked by the match logic; a mismatch is ignored until the next start. On a match INTFLAG.AMATCH is set and SCL is held low until software clears AMATCH, so software has unlimited time; with SCLSM = 1 the CTRLB.ACKACT acknowledge has already been sent. STATUS.DIR gives the direction and changes only on a valid address. STATUS.COLL set means the last packet addressed to the slave collided; on a collision SDA and SCL are released silently, so the next AMATCH is the first sign (this follows the SMBus Address Resolution Protocol). With SCLSM = 0, for a master read (DIR = 1) an ACK makes the slave set INTFLAG.DRDY to ask for data; for a master write (DIR = 0) an ACK makes it wait for data, repeated start or stop. After a NACK it waits for a new start. Command CTRLB.CMD = 3 serves both directions, acting on DIR, and writing one to AMATCH also sends the ACKACT acknowledge.

With SCLSM = 0 the slave then receives a byte or sends one written to DATA; each byte sets INTFLAG.DRDY, and a received byte is acknowledged per CTRLB.ACKACT. On a received byte SCL is held low until software acts. After a sent byte with a NACK the slave must release SDA and expect a stop or repeated start. A stop sets INTFLAG.PREC and the slave returns to idle.
Set to High-speed (CTRLA.SPEED = 0x2) with SCLSM = 1, the slave switches by itself: on a start, a master code and a NACK it enters High-speed mode and sets STATUS.HS, staying there until a stop.

With ADDR.TENBITEN = 1 the two address bytes after a start are checked as a 10-bit address; the first byte is always acknowledged and the second raises the address interrupt. A write continues with data. A read continues with a repeated start and 11110 ADDR[9:8] 1, which raises a second address interrupt with DIR set; the slave matches it because it was addressed by the preceding 10-bit address.

With CTRLB.GCMD set and 7-bit addressing, a stop raises the STOP interrupt if the slave was addressed since the previous stop. In a group command the master addresses several devices in one transmission with repeated starts and one final stop, at which every addressed device starts its command.

Three hardware SCL-low time-outs run from GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW, which must come from a 32 kHz oscillator. TTIMEOUT: one SCL low period of 25-35 ms, turned on by CTRLA.LOWTOUTEN. TLOW:SEXT: a total of 25 ms by which a slave stretches the clock low over one message, start to stop, turned on by CTRLA.SEXTTOEN. TLOW:MEXT: a total clock stretch of 10 ms by the master inside one byte, measured from start, or an ACK, to the next ACK or the stop; CTRLA.MEXTTOEN turns it on. An SMBus-compatible SDA hold time is also available.
In smart mode reading DATA.DATA sends the ACK or NACK held in CTRLB.ACKACT by itself.

CTRLA.PINOUT selects 4-wire mode for master or slave: the internal I2C tri-state drivers are bypassed, SDA_OUT and SCL_OUT appear on their own pads, and joining an I2C bus then takes an outside tri-state driver that meets the I2C specification.
With CTRLB.QCEN set the interrupt flag is set right after the slave acknowledges the address; software then issues a stop or a repeated start through CTRLB.CMD or ADDR.ADDR.

DMA needs smart mode (CTRLB.SMEN). Slave: an address match raises the address interrupt, and after it is served data moves by DMA; requests are RX (master write data received, cleared by reading DATA) and TX (data needed for a master read, cleared by writing DATA). Master: write ADDR with the address, ADDR.LEN and ADDR.LENEN = 1; LEN sets 0 to 255 data bytes, moved by DMA, followed by an automatic NACK (on reads) and stop. If the slave NACKs a master write before LEN bytes, a stop is sent and STATUS.LENERR and INTFLAG.ERROR are set. Master requests are RX (read data received, cleared by reading DATA) and TX (write data needed, cleared by writing DATA).

Slave sources: Error, Data Ready, Address Match and Stop Received. Master sources: Error, Slave on Bus and Master on Bus. Each has an INTFLAG bit, is enabled through INTENSET and INTENCLR, and all share one line. There are no events.

As master GCLK_SERCOMx_CORE keeps running in idle, and in standby too with CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1; any interrupt can wake the device. With RUNSTDBY = 0 the clock stops when the current transaction ends. As slave, RUNSTDBY = 1 lets Address Match wake the device; with RUNSTDBY = 0 all reception is dropped.

A synchronized write sets its SYNCBUSY bit and clears it when done; another synchronized access meanwhile gives a peripheral bus error. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST (SYNCBUSY.SWRST), CTRLA.ENABLE (SYNCBUSY.ENABLE), and SYNCBUSY.SYSOP for writes to STATUS.BUSSTATE, and in master operation to ADDR.ADDR and DATA.

The TC is a timer/counter of 8, 16 or 32 bits, with its prescaler, compare/capture channels and the logic that runs them. It counts prescaled clock pulses or events. With its channels it time-stamps input events to capture frequency and pulse width, and generates waveforms: frequency generation and single-slope PWM. It has one input event, interrupts and output events on overflow/underflow and on compare match or capture, and can use and trigger DMA.

The TC runs in any sleep mode in which its clock source runs; its interrupts wake the device and its events act without waking it. CLK_TCx_APB is switched in the Power Manager. TC instances form even/odd pairs counted from TC1, and the two of a pair share one generic clock GCLK_TCx, so the two cannot use different clocks. GCLK_TCx is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some register accesses need synchronization. DMA requests go to the DMAC, the interrupt line to the NVIC, and events through the EVSYS. In debug halt the TC stops unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. Every writable register can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS, READREQ, COUNT, PER and CCx; protection is lifted while the CPU is halted in debug and does not apply to an external debugger. No analog connections.

The counter counts EVSYS events or GCLK_TCx pulses through the prescaler. Its value goes to the compare/capture channels, to be compared with set values or captured on an event. The counter size (8, 16 or 32 bits) and clock set its range and resolution. It counts up or down; by default it counts up continuously and wraps to zero at the top value. In compare mode a match on CCx can toggle output pins, for frequency and PWM generation; capture mode measures period and pulse width.

CTRLA (except RUNSTDBY, ENABLE and SWRST) and EVCTRL.EVACT can be written only while the TC is disabled; the protected CTRLA bits may be written together with ENABLE = 1 but not with ENABLE = 0. Before enabling: enable CLK_TCx_APB; choose 8, 16 or 32 bits in CTRLA.MODE (16 bits by default); choose CTRLA.WAVEGEN; optionally a prescaler (CTRLA.PRESCALER) and its synchronization (CTRLA.PRESYNC); one-shot (CTRLBSET.ONESHOT); counting down (CTRLBSET.DIR); capture channels (CTRLC.CPTEN); inverted outputs (CTRLC.INVEN). CTRLA.ENABLE enables; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables. Disable the TC before resetting it to avoid undefined behaviour.

GCLK_TC passes through a prescaler with outputs from 1 to 1/1024 (GCLK_TC divided by 1, 2, 4, 8, 64, 256 or 1024). The prescaler counts to the chosen value and toggles its output. Above one, CTRLA.PRESYNC chooses whether the prescaler resets to zero or keeps counting on an overflow or underflow, and whether the counter wraps on the next GCLK_TC pulse or the next prescaled pulse (CLK_TC_CNT). Counted events bypass the prescaler.

CTRLA.MODE selects the counter, 16 bits by default. COUNT8 has its own period register PER, usable as top value for waveforms. COUNT16 has no period register. COUNT32 joins two 16-bit TCs of a pair: the even instance is the master and the odd one the slave, shown by STATUS.SLAVE. The slave's registers do not reflect the 32-bit counter, writes to them do not affect it, and normal access to the slave's COUNT and CCx is not allowed.

Counting up, the counter wraps to zero the cycle after reaching top; counting down, it wraps to top after zero. In one-shot mode it stops after a wrap. CTRLBSET.DIR = 1 counts down and CTRLBCLR.DIR = 1 counts up. Reaching top or zero sets INTFLAG.OVF, and with EVCTRL.OVFEO = 1 also gives an event. COUNT can be read or written; it starts at zero unless written, or unless the TC was stopped while counting down and reloaded at top. The stop command (CTRLBSET.CMD) halts the counter at its value, clears all waveforms and sets STATUS.STOP.

operation.topic: TC retrigger, count and start actions
operation.text: Retrigger comes from the CTRLBSET.CMD command or the EVCTRL.EVACT retrigger action. On a running counter it wraps to top or zero by direction; on a stopped counter it resumes from COUNT. With the retrigger event action enabled, enabling the TC does not start it: it starts on the next event and restarts on each following one. The count action increments or decrements on each event according to CTRLBSET.DIR. The start action postpones the start after enabling until the next event or a software retrigger; once running, events have no effect.

In compare mode the counter is compared continuously with each CCx. For a waveform on a pin: choose a waveform mode, optionally invert it (CTRLC.INVx), and enable the PORT multiplexer. A match sets INTFLAG.MCx on the next rising edge of CLK_TC_CNT, with an interrupt and/or event if INTENSET.MCx and/or EVCTRL.MCEOx is set. CTRLA.WAVEGEN picks normal frequency (NFRQ), match frequency (MFRQ), normal PWM (NPWM) or match PWM (MPWM). In NFRQ and NPWM the top value depends on the mode: PER in 8-bit mode, changeable by writing PER; the counter maximum in 16- and 32-bit modes.
In NFRQ, WO[x] toggles and the channel flag is set each time COUNT equals CCx. In MFRQ, CC0 is the top value and WO[0] toggles at each overflow or underflow.

In PWM the CCx registers set the duty cycle. Counting up, WO[x] is set at the start or at the match with top and cleared at the match with CCx; counting down, it is cleared at start or at top and set at the CCx match. In MPWM CC0 is the top value and a negative pulse appears on WO[0] at each overflow or underflow.

The top value can change while the counter runs. Counting down, a new top written when the counter is near zero may be missed through synchronization delay and the old top reloaded, giving one extra cycle before the new top applies. Counting up, a new top lower than the current count is missed and the counter runs on to its maximum before wrapping.

Capture needs the event input enabled (EVCTRL.TCEI) and the channels enabled in CTRLC.CPTENx. Event capture stores the count on any EVSYS event; all channels share one event line, so enable one channel at a time for it. A new capture while the channel's capture flag is still set has nowhere to go and sets INTFLAG.ERR.

EVCTRL.EVACT = PPW captures the period T into CC0 and the pulse width tp into CC1; PWP captures tp into CC0 and T into CC1. Two captures are made, one on each edge, and the counter restarts on one of them: the rising edge, or the falling edge with EVCTRL.TCINV = 1. The captured event must be asynchronous. CTRLC.CPTEN = 0x3 enables both channels; if only one measurement is needed the other channel is free. A capture while the flag is still set sets INTFLAG.ERR.

With CTRLBSET.ONESHOT set (cleared by CTRLBCLR.ONESHOT) the counter stops at the next overflow or underflow; STATUS.STOP is set by hardware and the waveform outputs go to zero. A retrigger command, retrigger event or start event restarts it, and STATUS.STOP clears.

DMA requests: OVF, set on an update condition (overflow or underflow) and cleared the next clock cycle; MCx, for a compare channel set on each match and cleared the next cycle, for a capture channel set when CCx holds valid data and cleared when CCx is read. With the OVF request the new value lands after the update, after DMA and synchronization delay, so if COUNT has already passed the new PER or CCx no match occurs. With the MCx request, writing a CCx beyond the current count in the counting direction can match again before the overflow, start the next transfer, and drop the previous value from WO[x].

Interrupt sources: overflow/underflow (OVF), the compare or capture channels, capture overflow error (ERR) and synchronization ready (SYNCRDY), each with an INTFLAG bit, enabled through INTENSET and INTENCLR, on one shared line. Output events: overflow/underflow (OVF) and match or capture (MC), enabled in EVCTRL.MCEO. Event actions, chosen in EVCTRL.EVACT: start, retrigger, increment or decrement (by direction), capture event, capture period, capture pulse width. EVCTRL.TCEI enables input events.
The TC can work in any sleep mode; in standby it needs CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1. It can wake the device by interrupt from any sleep mode or act through the EVSYS.

During synchronization STATUS.SYNCBUSY is set; INTFLAG.SYNCRDY can signal the end. A synchronized access while SYNCBUSY is set stalls the bus: it completes, but the CPU waits and interrupts stay pending. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, and the registers CTRLBCLR, CTRLBSET, CTRLC, COUNT, PERIOD and CCx. The same registers are synchronized on read.

The TCC is a timer/counter for control applications, built from a counter, its prescaler, a set of compare/capture channels and the logic that controls them. It counts clock pulses or events, time-stamps input events to capture frequency and pulse width, and generates frequency and PWM waveforms. Its waveform extensions target power control: motors, ballasts, LEDs, H-bridges, power converters and similar: low- and high-side outputs with optional dead time, a synchronized bit pattern across the outputs, and fault options that disable or shut down external drivers in a safe, deterministic way. The three instances differ as the configuration summary shows.

Up to four compare/capture channels with double-buffered period and compare/capture values and a circular buffer on the period and compare registers. Waveforms: frequency, single-slope PWM, and dual-slope PWM with half-cycle reload. Capture of events, frequency and pulse width. Waveform extensions: distribution of channel outputs across pins, low- and high-side outputs with programmable dead time, output swap and pattern generation with double buffering, and dithering. Fault protection: two recoverable and two non-recoverable fault sources, the debugger being able to act as a non-recoverable fault. Two counter input events and one input event per channel; three counter output events (count, retrigger, overflow) and one compare match/capture output event per channel. Interrupts on overflow and retrigger, compare match/capture and fault detection. DMA use and DMA triggering.

The TCC runs in any sleep mode where its clock source runs; its interrupts wake the device and its events act through the EVSYS without waking it. CLK_TCCx_APB is switched in the Power Manager. GCLK_TCCx must be set up in GCLK before use and is asynchronous to the bus clock, so some writes need synchronization. DMA requests go to the DMAC and the interrupt line to the NVIC. In debug halt the TCC stops unless DBGCTRL keeps it running. Every writable register can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG, STATUS, PER and PERB, CCx and CCBx, WAVE and WAVEB, and PATT and PATTB; protection does not apply to an external debugger. No analog connections.

An instance holds as many as four compare/capture channels (CCx), called compare channels when comparing and capture channels when capturing. COUNT, PER and PERB, CCx and CCBx are 16- or 24-bit, by instance. Every buffer register carries a BV (buffer valid) flag, set while it holds a new value. The counter is compared continuously with TOP, with zero and with each CCx; the comparisons give interrupts, DMA requests and events and set waveform period and pulse width. The counter runs from the prescaled GCLK_TCCx or from EVSYS events, and capture inputs come from the EVSYS.

Recoverable faults act on the channel outputs from events: restarting or halting the period, shortening the active pulse, or blocking the output while the fault lasts; uses include current-sense regulation and zero-crossing or demagnetization retriggering. They share the MCE0 and MCE1 event inputs, use only asynchronous events when enabled, and can be filtered digitally and/or blanked to reject glitches. A non-recoverable fault forces the outputs to a preset safe value, for instant shut-down of high-current or high-voltage drives. It shares the count event inputs TCE0 and TCE1; unfiltered, it acts on the outputs immediately and asynchronously, even without a clock.

Some instances carry up to six further units in series for power switching. The output matrix (OTMX) routes channel outputs across the pins in several layouts. Dead-time insertion (DTI) splits each of the four lower OTMX outputs into a non-inverted low side (LS) and an inverted high side (HS) that never overlap, with optional dead time between them. SWAP exchanges the LS and HS pins, for fast-decay motor control. The pattern generator sets constant levels on the outputs, synchronized to updates, for stepper and full-bridge control.

CTRLA (except RUNSTDBY, ENABLE and SWRST), FCTRLA and FCTRLB, WEXCTRL, DRVCTRL and EVCTRL can be written only while the TCC is disabled; the protected CTRLA bits may be written together with ENABLE = 1 but not with ENABLE = 0. Before enabling: enable CLK_TCCx_APB and, for capture, set CTRLA.CAPTEN for the channel. Before or after enabling: CTRLA.PRESCALER, CTRLA.PRESCSYNC, down-counting by CTRLBSET.DIR, the waveform in WAVE.WAVEGEN, output polarity in WAVE.POL, and per-channel output inversion in DRVCTRL.INVEN. CTRLA.ENABLE enables; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables. Disable the TCC before resetting it to avoid undefined behaviour.

GCLK_TCCx feeds a prescaler with outputs from 1 to 1/1024 (GCLK_TCC divided by 1, 2, 4, 8, 64, 256 or 1024); it counts to the chosen value and toggles its output. Above one, CTRLA.PRESYNC chooses whether the prescaler resets or keeps counting on an external retrigger, and whether the counter wraps on the next GCLK_TCC pulse or the next prescaled pulse (CLK_TCC_CNT). Counted events bypass the prescaler.

On each CLK_TCC_CNT cycle the counter clears, reloads, increments or decrements; a clear or reload ends one cycle and starts the next. Counting up, reaching TOP clears it to zero on the next cycle; counting down, reaching zero reloads it from PER. Each match with TOP or zero sets INTFLAG.OVF, usable for an interrupt, DMA request or event; with CTRLBSET.ONESHOT set it also stops the counter. CTRLBCLR.DIR = 1 counts up and CTRLBSET.DIR = 1 counts down. COUNT can be written while running, and the write wins over count, clear or reload; the direction can change while running too; settings take effect after synchronization. The counter must run in normal operation when it is the time base for capture channels.

Stop (CTRLBSET.CMD = 0x2): the counter holds its value, waveforms go to the state set by DRVCTRL.NREx and NRVx, and STATUS.STOP is set. Pause (EVCTRL.EVACT1 = 0x3): the counter holds and waveforms keep their state until a start event (EVCTRL.EVACT0 = 0x3). Retrigger (CTRLBSET.CMD = 0x1 or EVACTn = 0x1): while counting, the counter reloads or clears by direction, INTFLAG.TRG is set and, with EVCTRL.TRGEO, an event is sent; when stopped it resumes from COUNT; with a retrigger event action, enabling does not start the counter, which starts on the next event and restarts on each following one. Start (EVACT0 = 0x3): starts a stopped counter, no effect while counting; enabling waits for the event or a software retrigger, and later events do not restart it. Count (EVACT0 = 0x5): each event counts up or down by direction. Direction (EVACT1 = 0x2): the event level, on an asynchronous path, overrides DIR. Increment (EVACT0 = 0x4): TCE0 increments regardless of DIR. Decrement (EVACT1 = 0x4): TCE1 decrements regardless of DIR. Non-recoverable fault (EVACTn = 0x7): the counter stops and the outputs follow DRVCTRL.NREx and NRVx; TCE0 and TCE1 must be asynchronous events. Off (EVACTn = 0x0): enabling the counter starts it.

Channels compare by default and must be reconfigured to capture. In compare mode the counter is compared with each CCx continuously. The buffer CCBx double-buffers CCx: it is copied at the UPDATE condition, which prevents odd-length, asymmetric pulses and keeps the output glitch-free. For a waveform on a pin: choose WAVE.WAVEGEN, optionally invert WO[x] with DRVCTRL.INVENx, and enable the PORT multiplexer. A match sets INTFLAG.MCx on the next rising edge of CLK_TCC_COUNT; INTENSET.MCx gives an interrupt and EVCTRL.MCEOx an event, both possible together, and the same match gives a DMA request. Modes: normal frequency (NFRQ), match frequency (MFRQ), single-slope PWM (NPWM), and dual-slope PWM with interrupt/event at top (DSTOP), at zero (DSBOTTOM), at both (DSBOTH), or critical at zero (DSCRITICAL). In MFRQ CC0 sets TOP; in every other mode PER does. Dual-slope modes update when the counter reaches zero; the others on wrap, overflow, underflow or retrigger.
NFRQ: PER sets the period; WO[x] toggles and the channel flag is set at each match of COUNT with CCx. MFRQ: CC0 sets the period and WO[0] toggles at each update.

PER sets the period and CCx the duty cycle. Counting up, WO[x] is set at start or at the TOP match and cleared at the CCx match; counting down, it is cleared at start or at TOP and set at the CCx match.

PER sets TOP and CCx the duty cycle; the counter runs from zero up to PER and back down. WO[x] is set at the match while counting up and cleared at the match while counting down. The interrupt/event comes at TOP and/or zero according to the mode; DSBOTH adds a second update at TOP. Dual-slope reaches a lower maximum frequency than single-slope. TOP sets the resolution, at least 1 bit (TOP = 0x00000001); with TOP = 1 and no prescaling the output reaches half the TCC clock frequency. In DSTOP, DSBOTTOM and DSBOTH with TOP below MAX/2, the MSB of CCx chooses the ramp on which the match interrupt or event is given: rising for 0, falling for 1.
Critical mode makes centred pulses that need not be aligned: PER sets the period, CCx sets the output edge while counting up and CC(x + CC_NUM/2) the edge while counting down.

WAVE.POLx applies in every waveform mode. In single- and dual-slope PWM it moves each channel's pulse edge to the start or the end of the cycle. In normal and match frequency, POLx is the initial output state.

PATT, WAVE, PER and CCx are double buffered; STATUS holds a buffer valid bit for each (PATTBV, WAVEBV, PERBV, CCBVx), set while the buffer holds a value to copy. With double buffering on (CTRLBCLR.LUPD = 1) and PER and CCx used for compare, the BV bit sets when the buffer is written and clears at the update. Both the registers and their buffers (PATTB, WAVEB, PERB, CCBx) are in the register map, so buffering is optional; CTRLBSET.LUPD = 1 turns it off, for initialization or to bypass the buffer. In NFRQ, MFRQ or PWM counting down (CTRLBSET.DIR = 1), a write to PERB also writes PER at once if CTRLB.LUPD is zero, or later at the moment LUPD returns to zero.

The period changes by writing PER or PERB. Unbuffered, a PER write takes effect after the synchronization delay, and when counting up in any mode a new top lower than the current count is missed, so the counter wraps at its maximum. With buffering, PERB can be written at any time and PER is always loaded at the update, which prevents the wrap and odd waveforms.

Capture needs EVCTRL.MCEIx for the channel's event input and CTRLA.CPTENx for the channel. Each channel has its own event line, so several captures can run together. For capture CCBx and CCx form a FIFO: CCBx moves into CCx whenever CCx is empty or has been read, and the buffer valid flag sets the channel flag, with optional interrupt, event or DMA request. A capture while MCx and the buffer valid flag are both set has nowhere to go and sets INTFLAG.ERR.

With EVCTRL.EVACT1 = PPW the period goes to CC0 and the pulse width tp to CC1; with PWP, tp to CC0 and the period to CC1. Two captures are made, one on each edge, and the counter restarts on the edge chosen by EVCTRL.TCEINV1. The captured event must be asynchronous. Enable CC0 and CC1 with CTRLA.CPTENx; if one measurement suffices the other channel is free. A capture while the flag is still set sets INTFLAG.ERR. In dual-slope PWM with TOP below MAX/2, the CCx MSB records CTRLB.DIR to show the ramp of the capture: rising for 0, falling for 1.

With CTRLBSET.ONESHOT set (cleared by CTRLBCLR.ONESHOT) the counter stops at the next overflow or underflow; STATUS.STOP is set and the outputs take the DRVCTRL.NREx and NRVx values. A retrigger command, retrigger event or start event restarts it and clears STATUS.STOP.
PER and CC0 to CC3 can run as circular buffers: at each update PER or CCx is copied into its buffer register. The circular buffers serve RAMP2, RAMP2A and DSBOTH operation.

Dithering adds extra clock cycles to some compare matches, one at a time, across a frame of 16, 32 or 64 PWM cycles, raising the accuracy of the average pulse width or period; a blue-noise sequence keeps flicker low. CTRLA.RESOLUTION selects DITH4 (every 16 PWM frames), DITH5 (32) or DITH6 (64). The low DITHERCY bits of COUNT, PER and CCx give the extra cycles per frame (the 4 low bits in DITH4) and the remaining bits the value itself. A cycle gets an extra clock when ((MASK AND (cycle × dithercy)) + dithercy) > MASK, with MASK = 0x0f, 0x1f or 0x3f for DITH4, DITH5 or DITH6.

Three ramp operations, all in single-slope PWM. RAMP1 is the default single-slope PWM. RAMP2 interleaves two counter cycles, for PFC, half-bridge and push-pull SMPS: in cycle A the odd channel outputs are off, in cycle B the even ones. The ramp index changes at each update and can be set by CTRLBSET.IDXCMD. Standard RAMP2: PER sets both ramp periods, different for A and B with the circular buffer (CIPEREN); a two-channel TCC can make two outputs, or one output with the other channel capturing. Alternate RAMP2A: CC0 drives both WO[0] and WO[1] with its circular buffer on, both with the same polarity, and channel 1 can capture.

operation.topic: TCC recoverable fault inputs and filtering
operation.text: Fault A and Fault B act on channels CC0 and CC1; they can restart or halt the counter and clamp the outputs inactive while the fault lasts or from the first valid fault to the end of the cycle. The first two channel input events (MC0, MC1) are the Fault A and Fault B inputs, on asynchronous EVSYS channels. Three filters, usable alone or together. Input filter: detection is asynchronous by default and acts at once, even in sleep without a clock; FCTRLn.FILTERVAL adds a digital filter that delays the event by FILTERVAL clock cycles and drops narrower events. Blanking: ignores the fault input for FCTRLn.BLANKVAL cycles after a chosen output edge (FCTRLn.BLANK); the longest blanking is 256 / (96 × 10^6) = 2.66 µs at a 96 MHz GCLK_TCCx and 256 / (1 × 10^6) = 256 µs at 1 MHz. Qualification (FCTRLn.QUAL): the fault input is ignored while its channel output is inactive.

Actions are set separately for Fault A and Fault B and can be combined. Keep (FCTRLn.KEEP): the channel output is clamped to zero while the fault lasts and released at the start of the first cycle after it ends. Restart (FCTRLn.RESTART): the current cycle stops and a new one starts, outputs inactive while the fault lasts; in RAMP2 the cycle index changes, and Fault A and Fault B are honoured only in cycles A and B respectively. Capture (FCTRLn.CAPTURE): the count is captured at the fault: CAPT, a normal capture with an interrupt each time; CAPTMIN and CAPTMAX keep the lowest or highest value and flag each new extreme; LOCMIN and LOCMAX capture every time but flag only a value lower or higher than the previous; DERIV0 is LOCMIN or LOCMAX. Hardware halt (FCTRLn.HALT = HW): the counter halts and the cycle stretches while the fault lasts, the channel output inactive, and resumes after; with restart also on, it restarts when the fault ends; in RAMP2 and RAMP2A the cycle index changes at each new cycle. Software halt (HALT = SWHALT): as hardware halt, but restarting also needs the STATUS FAULTn bit cleared.

A non-recoverable fault forces every compare output to the level in DRVCTRL.NRE and DRVCTRL.NRV. The fault inputs EV0 and EV1 are enabled by EVCTRL.EVACT0 and EVACT1. DRVCTRL.FILTERVALn adds a digital filter against glitches; detection then becomes synchronous and the action is delayed by the filter's clock cycles.

After the recoverable fault stage come OTMX, DTI, SWAP and the pattern generator. DTI and SWAP work on pin pairs: slice x acts on WO[x] and WO[WO_NUM/2 + x]. Output matrix configurations: 0x0, the default, puts channel n on OTMX[n] and repeats the channels modulo their number when there are more outputs than channels; 0x1 repeats them modulo half the number of channels, giving the lower channels twice the outputs, for example a full bridge from two channels, with pattern generation overriding some outputs for all-quadrant drive; 0x2 sends CC0 to every pin, for a stepper motor with pattern generation; 0x3 sends CC0 to the first output and CC1 to all others, which, with pattern generation and the fault extension, can run as many as seven LED strings behind a boost stage.

DTI makes an off time, the dead time, during which both the non-inverted low side and the inverted high side are low, so they never switch together. Four identical generators serve the four lowest channels, sharing one dead-time register independent of the side settings. An 8-bit counter counts down one per peripheral clock to zero, holding both outputs off while non-zero. A rising edge of the OTMX output reloads it from DTLS and a falling edge from DTHS.

The pattern generator puts a synchronized bit pattern on its pins, mainly for BLDC, stepper and full-bridge commutation. PGE[7:0] enables the override per output and PGV[7:0] gives its value, each with a buffer (PGEB, PGVB) loaded at the UPDATE condition like the other double-buffered registers; when synchronization is not needed, PATT.PGE and PATT.PGV can be written directly.

DMA requests: OVF, set at an update condition (overflow, underflow or retrigger); MCx, for a compare channel set at each match, for a capture channel set when CCx holds valid data and cleared when CCx is read.

Interrupt sources: overflow/underflow (OVF), retrigger (TRG), count (CNT, see EVCTRL.CNTSEL), capture overflow error (ERR), debug fault state (DFS), recoverable faults (FAULTn), non-recoverable faults (FAULTx) and the compare match or capture channels (MCx); each has an INTFLAG bit, enabled through INTENSET and INTENCLR, on one shared line. Output events: OVF, TRG, CNT and MCx, each enabled by its EVCTRL.xxEO bit. Channel input event (MCx) actions: capture, or a recoverable fault. Counter event 1 (TCCx EV1) actions: retrigger, direction control, stop, decrement, period and pulse-width capture, non-recoverable fault. Counter event 0 (TCCx EV0) actions: retrigger, count up or down by direction, start (on the rising edge; later events do not restart it and it runs on the prescaled GCLK_TCCx to TOP or zero), increment regardless of direction, count on each prescaled clock while an asynchronous event is active, and non-recoverable fault. EVCTRL.EVACT0 and EVACT1 select the counter actions; EVCTRL.MCEIx and TCEIx enable the input actions, which apply to every event connected.
The TCC can work in any sleep mode; standby needs CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1. It can wake the device by interrupt from any sleep mode or act through the EVSYS.

Accessing a synchronized register sets its SYNCBUSY bit, cleared when done; an access while that bit is set triggers a hardware interrupt. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST and CTRLA.ENABLE, and the registers CTRLBCLR, CTRLBSET, STATUS, PATT, PATTB, WAVE, WAVEB, COUNT, PER, PERB, CCx and CCBx.

The USB module is a USB 2.1 device. It has 8 endpoint addresses, each with an IN and an OUT endpoint, 16 in all, each configurable as control, interrupt, bulk or isochronous. Endpoint configuration and data buffers live in system SRAM at locations software chooses, sized by the endpoints in use; a built-in DMA moves data to and from RAM during transactions without the CPU or the DMAC. Ping-pong operation uses the IN and OUT endpoints of one address in one direction for double buffering. Multi-packet transfer sends a payload larger than the endpoint size as several packets without software. On bus suspend the device can enter any sleep mode, and bus resume wakes it from any sleep mode.

USB 2.1 compatible embedded device; full speed (12 Mbit/s) and low speed (1.5 Mbit/s); Link Power Management (LPM-L1); transceivers on chip, with their pull-up and pull-down resistors and the series resistors also internal; a 1 kHz SOF clock on an external pin. Device mode: 8 IN and 8 OUT endpoints, no endpoint size limits, the internal DMA, multi-packet transfers and two banks available on every endpoint, feedback endpoints, and crystal-less clocking.

The USB pins and the 1 kHz SOF output must be assigned to the USB function in the I/O controller first. The USB runs in any sleep mode where its clock source runs and its interrupts wake the device. CLK_USB_AHB is switched in the Power Manager; GCLK_USB must be set up in GCLK before use and is asynchronous to it, so some writes need synchronization. The built-in DMA needs no CPU or DMAC. Interrupt lines go to the NVIC; no events, no analog connections. In debug halt the USB keeps running. Every writable register can be PAC-protected except INTFLAG and EPINTFLAG; protection does not apply to an external debugger.

GCLK_USB must be 48 MHz ± 0.25% for low- and full-speed operation, and CLK_USB_AHB at least 8 MHz to keep up with the 12 Mbit/s full-speed rate. A digital phase-locked loop in the module recovers the clock within the USB jitter specification. Crystal-less device operation uses the USB clock recovery mode of the DFLL48M.

The DP/DM output drivers are trimmed by calibration values from production test. Software loads them from the NVM software calibration area and writes them to PADCAL before enabling the USB, to reach the specified accuracy.

After a hardware reset the USB is idle: disabled (CTRLA.ENABLE cleared), its clock stopped, the pad in suspend and its internal state and registers reset. Load PADCAL with the calibration values first. CTRLB.SPDCONF can set pads and speed before enabling; it applies once enabled. CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 enables the USB, which enters device mode per CTRLA.MODE; writing 0 disables it at any time. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register and disables the USB.

CTRLB.DETACH = 0 attaches the device to the host and 1 detaches it. The host reads the device descriptor at address zero, sends a USB reset, then assigns an address; software writes it to DADD.DADD and sets DADD.ADDEN to accept traffic to it. A USB reset clears DADD.ADDEN.

Endpoint data can sit anywhere in RAM; the controller reaches it through its AHB master using endpoint descriptors whose base address software writes to DESCADD. Before use, set the direction and type in EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1 and initialize the descriptor so no random RAM is read: PCKSIZE.SIZE matching the size reported to the host, and ADDR pointing at the data buffer. INTFLAG.RAMACER is set on a RAM access underflow during an IN data stage. Disabling an endpoint clears its EPINTENCLR/SET, EPINTFLAG and EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0 and STALLRQ1.

Software gives the size and address of a RAM buffer for an endpoint, and the module splits it into the needed USB transactions on its own, cutting interrupts and software work. Otherwise transactions behave as single IN and OUT transactions.

A bus reset comes from the host and is handled by hardware. It clears EPCFG (except endpoint 0), FNUM, DADD, EPINTENCLR/SET, EPINTFLAG, EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0 and STALLRQ1, EPINTSMRY and CTRLB.UPRSM. At its end INTFLAG.EORST is set.
On a SOF token the frame number is stored in FNUM.FNUM and INTFLAG.SOF is set; a CRC or bit-stuff error sets FNUM.FNCERR.

A SETUP token is dropped if its address is not DADD.DADD, if the endpoint is disabled in EPCFG, or if EPCFG.EPTYPE0 is not control. Otherwise the module reads ADDR from the descriptor and waits for DATA0; any other PID or a PID error returns it to idle. If EPINTFLAG.RXSTP is zero the data is written to ADDR regardless of EPSTATUS.BK0RDY; bytes beyond PCKSIZE.SIZE are dropped but the packet is still checked, and software must never report to the host an endpoint size larger than PCKSIZE.SIZE. A bit-stuff or CRC error returns to idle. On success the device ACKs and writes the byte count, without CRC, to PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT; with exactly SIZE bytes no CRC is stored, with SIZE − 1 the first CRC byte is stored, with SIZE − 2 or fewer both are. Then EPSTATUS.DTGLOUT, DTGLIN, CURRBK and BK0RDY are set, BK1RDY and STALLRQ0/1 cleared, and RXSTP set, with an interrupt if enabled in EPINTENSET.

An OUT token is dropped if its address does not match, the endpoint is disabled, or EPCFG.EPTYPE0 is not OUT. The module reads ADDR and waits for DATA0 or DATA1. With EPSTATUS.STALLRQ0 set the data is dropped and, except on isochronous endpoints, a STALL is returned and EPINTFLAG.STALL0 set. Isochronous endpoints accept both DATA0 and DATA1; others check the PID against EPSTATUS.DTGLOUT and on a mismatch drop the data but return ACK. With EPSTATUS.BK0RDY set the data is dropped, EPINTFLAG.TRFAIL0 and STATUS_BK.ERRORFLOW are set and, except on isochronous endpoints, NAK is returned. Data is written to ADDR, bytes beyond PCKSIZE.SIZE dropped, the packet checked; a bit-stuff or CRC error returns to idle, except that an isochronous endpoint stores the byte count and sets TRFAIL0 and STATUS_BK.CRCERR. On success the device ACKs (not on isochronous), stores the byte count and CRC bytes as for SETUP, sets EPSTATUS.BK0RDY, toggles DTGLOUT (not on isochronous) and sets EPINTFLAG.TRCPT0.

PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT counts the bytes received and, being updated after each transaction, must be zeroed for a new transfer. PCKSIZE.MULTI_PACKET_SIZE holds the total to receive and must be a multiple of PCKSIZE.SIZE, or excess data may land in SRAM used elsewhere. Each full-size packet adds SIZE to BYTE_COUNT and toggles DTGLOUT (not on isochronous). When BYTE_COUNT reaches MULTI_PACKET_SIZE, the last transaction, BK0RDY/BK1RDY and EPINTFLAG.TRCPT0/TRCPT1 are set.

An IN token is dropped if its address does not match, the endpoint is disabled, or EPCFG.EPTYPE1 is not IN. With EPSTATUS.STALLRQ1 set on a non-isochronous endpoint a STALL is returned and EPINTFLAG.STALL1 set. With EPSTATUS.BK1RDY clear, EPINTFLAG.TRFAIL1 is set and, except on isochronous endpoints, NAK is returned. Otherwise the data at ADDR is sent, as DATA0 on isochronous endpoints and as DATA0 or DATA1 by EPSTATUS.DTGLIN on others, PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT bytes followed by the CRC. Isochronous: BK1RDY clears and TRCPT1 sets. Others wait for an ACK; without one within 16 bit times the module returns to idle, with one it clears BK1RDY, sets TRCPT1 and toggles DTGLIN.

PCKSIZE.BYTE_COUNT holds the total to send and PCKSIZE.MULTI_PACKET_SIZE counts bytes sent; zero it for a new transfer. On each IN token, if BYTE_COUNT − MULTI_PACKET_SIZE is less than PCKSIZE.SIZE that remainder is sent, otherwise SIZE bytes. If BYTE_COUNT is a multiple of SIZE and AUTOZLP is set, a zero-length packet ends the transfer. A full packet adds SIZE to MULTI_PACKET_SIZE and toggles DTGLIN (not on isochronous); the short last packet adds its length, clears BK0/1RDY and sets EPINTFLAG.TRCPT0/1.

A ping-pong endpoint uses both banks of its address in one direction: one of EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1 is set to the direction and the other to Dual Bank. The enabled endpoint's buffer, address pointer and byte counter are bank 0 and the other direction's are bank 1. EPSTATUS.CURBK shows which bank the next transaction uses and updates after each one; TRCPT0/TRFAIL0 or TRCPT1/TRFAIL1 and BK0RDY or BK1RDY are set by the bank used. DTGLOUT and DTGLIN update only for the enabled direction. The second bank gives the CPU time to process data without the endpoint returning NAK.

A feedback endpoint shares an address with a data endpoint but has the opposite direction, as in explicit feedback for USB Audio, where it serves one or more isochronous data endpoints and takes the number of the first (lowest) one. It is made by giving the IN and OUT directions of one address different PCKSIZE.SIZE and EPCFG.EPTYPE0/1. Example: endpoint n IN with EPCFG.EPTYPE1 = Interrupt IN and PCKSIZE.SIZE = 64; endpoint n OUT with EPCFG.EPTYPE0 = Isochronous OUT and PCKSIZE.SIZE = 512.

The pad has two states: Idle, at low power, and Active. Detecting bus suspend sets INTFLAG.SUSPEND and puts the pad in Idle by itself; detecting a non-idle bus sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP and makes it Active. The pad also goes Idle when the USB is disabled or CTRLB.DETACH = 1, and returns to Active with CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 and CTRLB.DETACH = 0. SUSPEND clears on wake-up; WAKEUP is cleared by software to acknowledge it.

Remote wakeup, also called upstream resume, is the one request a device can start unprompted; the host should first have sent DEVICE_REMOTE_WAKEUP. It can be sent only after INTFLAG.SUSPEND has been set. Writing CTRLB.UPRSM = 1 sends an upstream resume, which the controller does after 5 ms of bus inactivity. Sending it sets INTFLAG.WAKEUP and clears SUSPEND; UPRSM clears when the resume has been sent. A host-initiated rebroadcast resume sets INTFLAG.EORSM when complete. If UPRSM is set while a host downstream resume is already under way, UPRSM is cleared and the request ignored.

CTRLB.LPMHDSK sets the handshake for LPM transactions. When an LPM transaction arrives on an enabled endpoint and is answered, the EXTREG field in bank 0 of that endpoint's descriptor is updated with the Best Effort Service Latency (BESL), bRemoteWake and bLinkState. After an ACK, INTFLAG.LPMSUSP is set and the transceiver suspends, 9 µs after the transaction. Stopping the USB clock while suspended saves more, and the MCU may sleep in any mode whose wake-up latency meets the host's BESL. Leaving LPM-L1 works as leaving suspend, with a shorter device-initiated remote wakeup. A NYET answer sets INTFLAG.LPMNYET, with an interrupt if INTENSET.LPMNYET is set; a STALL or no handshake sets nothing and the transaction is ignored.

Each endpoint n has flags EPINTFLAGn STALL, TRFAIL1, TRFAIL0, RXSTP, TRCPT1 and TRCPT0, each gated by its EPINTENSETn bit (STALL0/STALL1 for the stall flag); the result shows in EPINTSMRY as EPINTn, and all endpoints combine into the USB endpoint interrupt. Device flags in INTFLAG: LPMSUSP, LPMNYET, RAMACER, UPRSM, EORSM, WAKEUP, EORST, SOF, MSOF and SUSPEND, each gated by its INTENSET bit into the USB device interrupt; the endpoint and device interrupts form the USB interrupt. WAKEUP is asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode.

The ADC is a 12-bit converter running at up to 350 ksps, taking single-ended or differential inputs, with an optional gain stage from 1/2x to 16x. It has up to 32 inputs (25 positive and 10 negative, internal and external together) including five internal ones: the bandgap, the temperature sensor, the DAC, the scaled core supply and the scaled I/O supply. Results are signed or unsigned, 8, 10 or 12 bits (fewer bits convert faster), left- or right-adjusted, and averaging or oversampling with decimation gives up to a 16-bit result. Conversions start from software or from one event input, singly, continuously or scanning pins; a window monitor compares results to thresholds; hardware applies gain and offset correction; DMA can carry results away; the sampling time is selectable. The reference is internal or external, chosen by four bits; the reference range is 1 V to VDDANA − 0.6 V and the converted range of ADCx × GAIN is 0 V to −Vref.

The ADC pins are set up through PORT; pins AIN0 to AIN19 and the VREFA/VREFB pin are its analog inputs. It keeps running in any sleep mode in which its clock source runs, and its interrupts can wake the device. CLK_ADC_APB is gated in the Power Manager; the generic clock GCLK_ADC must be set up and enabled in GCLK first, and since it is asynchronous to the bus clock some register writes are synchronized. The DMA request needs the DMAC set up first, the interrupt line the NVIC. In debug halt the ADC stops unless DBGCTRL lets it run on. Every writable register except INTFLAG can be write-protected by the PAC; protection is off while the CPU is halted in debug or its reset is extended, and never applies to an external debugger.

For the specified accuracy, software must copy BIAS_CAL and LINEARITY_CAL to CALIB from the calibration values stored in the NVM software calibration area. Before enabling, choose and enable the asynchronous clock source (the GCLK_ADC source is chosen and enabled in SYSCTRL) and set the reference; discard the first conversion after a reference change and keep the other configuration registers steady while converting. CTRLA.ENABLE = 1 enables the ADC and 0 disables it. CTRLA.SWRST = 1 resets every register except DBGCTRL and disables the ADC; disable the ADC before resetting it.

The ADC samples the sources set in INPUTCTRL at a rate set by GCLK_ADC and its prescaler. A conversion starts by writing SWTRIG.START = 1 or from an automatic trigger; in free-running mode each conversion starts when the last ends, with no trigger. Each result overwrites RESULT. With more than one channel enabled, each result must be read when INTFLAG.RESRDY is set, otherwise INTFLAG.OVERRUN signals lost data. Interrupts are enabled through INTENSET.
CLK_ADC is GCLK_ADC divided by a 9-bit prescaler, set by CTRLB.PRESCALER[2:0] to divide by 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 or 512.

CTRLB.RESSEL selects 8-, 10- or 12-bit results; 12 bits after reset. Single-ended conversion gives the full 12 bits of positive values and needs the negative input grounded (internal GND, IOGND or a ground on a pin, chosen in INPUTCTRL); when the positive input can fall below the negative, use differential mode, set by CTRLB.DIFFMODE. Either runs as single conversions or free-running, which samples and converts continuously and sets INTFLAG.RESRDY after each conversion.

SWTRIG.START or the start event (EVCTRL.STARTEI) has to come one CLK_ADC_APB cycle or more ahead of the CLK_ADC cycle that begins the conversion. Sampling takes the first half of a CLK_ADC period; SAMPCTRL.SAMPLEN lengthens the sampling time. Without gain, a differential 12-bit conversion resolves its bits MSB first over the following CLK_ADC cycles; in single-ended mode an amplify phase follows sampling before the bits are resolved.

AVGCTRL.SAMPLENUM sets how many consecutive conversions are accumulated. Beyond 16 samples the sum no longer fits the 16-bit RESULT, so it is shifted right automatically. Averaging divides the sum by the count: the automatic shift plus a further right shift set in AVGCTRL.ADJRES; it improves accuracy in noise and divides the effective sample rate by SAMPLENUM. INTFLAG.RESRDY is set when the average is complete. Accumulating or averaging two or more samples needs CTRLB.RESSEL written to one.
Oversampling raises the resolution from 12 bits up to 16: n extra bits take 4^n accumulated samples and a right shift of n bits, made of the automatic shift plus AVGCTRL.ADJRES.

WINCTRL.WINMODE[2:0] chooses the window mode and WINLT and WINUT hold the lower and upper thresholds, read as signed values with differential input and unsigned otherwise. Only as many threshold bits count as CTRLB.RESSEL gives: in 8-bit mode the lower eight bits, and in differential mode the eighth bit is the sign even when the ninth is zero. A matching result sets INTFLAG.WINMON.

Offset error is the departure of the transfer function from the ideal line at zero input; gain error is the departure of the midpoint of the last output step from the ideal line once offset is removed. OFFSETCORR is subtracted from the conversion and the difference is multiplied by GAINCORR before it is written to RESULT; CTRLB.CORREN = 1 turns correction on. Correction adds 13 GCLK_ADC cycles of latency to a single conversion; in free-running mode only the first conversion is delayed, since correction takes less than a conversion.

The one DMA request, RESRDY, is set when a result is ready (or an average complete) and cleared by reading RESULT. Interrupt sources are RESRDY, OVERRUN, WINMON and SYNCRDY; RESRDY, WINMON and SYNCRDY are asynchronous and can wake the device from any sleep mode. Each flag in INTFLAG is enabled through INTENSET, disabled through INTENCLR and cleared by writing one to it. Output events are RESRDY and WINMON, enabled by EVCTRL.xxEO; input events start a conversion (START) or flush the ADC (FLUSH), enabled by EVCTRL.xxEI, and the action follows any connected event.

CTRLA.RUNSTDBY sets standby behaviour: at zero the ADC is off in standby, keeping its configuration, with its analog blocks unpowered, so a start-up delay follows wake-up; at one it keeps running and any enabled ADC interrupt can wake the CPU. While the CPU sleeps, only events can start conversions.

CLK_ADC_APB and GCLK_ADC are asynchronous. A synchronized access sets STATUS.SYNCBUSY until it completes, and the SYNCRDY interrupt can mark the end; an access needing synchronization while SYNCBUSY is set stalls the bus (and the CPU, with interrupts pending) until it finishes. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, CTRLB, SWTRIG, WINCTRL, INPUTCTRL, WINUT and WINLT. Synchronized on read: SWTRIG, INPUTCTRL and RESULT.

The analog comparator block holds one pair of comparators, COMP0 and COMP1, alike in behaviour with separate controls. Each compares a positive and a negative input and gives a digital output, one when positive minus negative is above zero. Inputs: four shared pins usable as positive or negative inputs, ground (for zero crossing), the bandgap, a 64-level VDDANA scaler per comparator, and the DAC. Propagation delay can be traded against current, hysteresis switched on or off, and each output brought to a pin, synchronous or not. Interrupts come on a rising or falling edge, a toggle or the end of a comparison; the pair can act as a window comparator with interrupts above, inside, below or outside the window. Events come from the comparator outputs and the window state. There is an optional digital filter on the output and a low-power single-shot mode.

The AC pins are set up through PORT and must be set for analog use, and an internal source (bandgap, DAC) must be set up and enabled before it is chosen as an input. The AC runs in any sleep mode in which its clock runs and its interrupts can wake the device. CLK_AC_APB is gated in the Power Manager. Two generic clocks serve it: GCLK_AC_DIG sets the sampling rate, and GCLK_AC_ANA keeps the input multiplexer resistance low when VDDANA is below 2.5 V; both must be enabled in GCLK first, and being asynchronous to CLK_AC_APB, some writes are synchronized.
