There is no DMA. The AC keeps running when the CPU halts in debug. Every writable register except CTRLB and INTFLAG can be write-protected by the PAC, never against an external debugger.

The comparators work alone (normal mode) or as a pair for window comparison. EVCTRL must be set before the AC is enabled, and each COMPCTRLx before its comparator is enabled; neither changes while enabled. COMPCTRLx selects single-shot or continuous (SINGLE), hysteresis (HYST), speed against power (SPEED), interrupt source (INTSEL), inputs (MUXPOS, MUXNEG) and filter (FLEN). CTRLA.ENABLE turns the AC on and each COMPCTRLx.ENABLE its comparator; clearing CTRLA.ENABLE stops both without clearing their ENABLE bits. CTRLA.SWRST resets every register except DEBUG and disables the AC.

After enabling, the comparator output is unavailable for a start-up time, measured automatically to follow temperature and supply and given in the electrical characteristics. Below 2.5 V supply the start-up also waits for the voltage doubler; with the supply sure to stay above 2.5 V, CTRLA.LPMUX = 1 turns the doubler off. Interrupts are chosen by COMPCTRLx.INTSEL: toggle, rising edge, falling edge or end of comparison (useful in single-shot mode to chain events whatever the output). Events follow the output state whether or not an interrupt is enabled.

With COMPCTRLx.SINGLE = 0 the comparator compares continuously and STATUSA.STATEx always holds the latest result. After the start-up time (which applies only to the first comparison) STATUSA updates, STATUSB.READYx sets and events and interrupts follow, until COMPCTRLx.ENABLE is cleared. Edges are found by comparing successive samples taken at the GCLK_AC_DIG rate; READYx rises 2 to 3 GCLK_AC cycles plus tSTARTUP after ENABLE is written. In sleep without a clock the comparator stays on and changes are detected asynchronously: a toggle makes the Power Manager start GCLK_AC_DIG to register events and interrupts, then stop it again unless the device is to wake.

With COMPCTRLx.SINGLE = 1 the comparator idles until CTRLB.STARTx = 1, which clears STATUSB.READYx, enables the comparator, waits the start-up time, makes one comparison, updates STATUSA, sets READYx and raises events and interrupts. Reading STATUSC starts a comparison on every single-shot comparator and stalls the bus until all enabled ones are ready; a comparator already busy finishes and is not restarted. With EVCTRL.COMPEIx = 1 an incoming event starts the comparison and clears READYx in the same way, each comparator on its own event. Edge detection compares the result with the previous one. Event-triggered comparisons work in sleep: the Power Manager starts GCLK_AC_DIG, the comparison runs, and comparator and clock stop again unless the device is to wake.

The positive input comes from a pin (AINx), chosen by COMPCTRLx.MUXPOS; the negative from a pin or one of the internal references common to both comparators, chosen by COMPCTRLx.MUXNEG. A pin used must have its digital input and output disabled in PORT. Inputs change only while the comparator is disabled; the multiplexers switch so as to limit crosstalk.

WINCTRL.WENx joins the pair into a window comparator; both must have the same COMPCTRLx.SINGLE. The same pin feeds both positive inputs and the two negative inputs set the window limits, either way round. STATUS.WSTATEx holds the window state. WINCTRL.WINTSELx[1:0] chooses an interrupt on going above, below, into or out of the window; events follow the inside/outside state regardless of the interrupt. The single comparator outputs, interrupts and events keep working. In single-shot window mode both comparators measure together, started by either CTRLB.STARTx or either event.

operation.topic: AC voltage doubler and VDDANA scaler
operation.text: A voltage doubler lowers the multiplexer resistance when the supply is below 2.5 V; it switches on and off by itself with the supply, adds start-up time when it is on, and CTRLA.LPMUX = 1 turns it off (saving power and start-up time) when the supply stays above 2.5 V. The VDDANA scaler gives each comparator its own reference, a fraction of the supply in 64 steps set by SCALERx.VALUE[5:0]; it is on while COMPCTRLx.MUXNEG = 5 and the comparator is enabled.

COMPCTRLx.HYST enables hysteresis per comparator, in continuous mode only. COMPCTRLx.SPEED sets the comparator's bias current, trading propagation delay against current and changing the start-up time. COMPCTRLx.FLEN picks no filter or a 3- or 5-sample majority filter: a change is accepted once N/2+1 out of the latest N samples match. Sampling runs at CLK_AC divided by CTRLA.PRESCALER and adds N−1 sampling cycles of delay; in continuous mode outputs then come every cycle, and a single-shot comparison ends after the Nth sample. In sleep, filtering works only for single-shot measurements and must be off for continuous measurements in sleep.

COMPCTRLx.OUT routes a comparator to its CMP[x] pin, either the raw asynchronous output or the CLK_AC-synchronized and filtered one. COMPCTRLx.SWAP exchanges the positive and negative inputs and inverts the output, so the input offset voltage can be measured or cancelled; it changes only while the comparator is disabled.

Interrupt sources are COMP0 and COMP1, as chosen by COMPCTRLx.INTSEL, and WIN0, as chosen by WINCTRL.WINTSEL[1:0]; each is enabled in INTENSET, disabled in INTENCLR and cleared by writing one to its INTFLAG bit. Output events are COMPEO0, COMPEO1 and WINEO0, enabled in EVCTRL. Input events start a single-shot measurement, or one in window mode, when EVCTRL.COMPEIx = 1; the comparison begins after the start-up time. In normal mode each comparator answers its own event; in window mode either event starts both.

CTRLA.RUNSTDBY sets standby behaviour: at zero the pair is off in standby, keeping its configuration, with its analog blocks unpowered, so a start-up delay follows wake-up; at one it keeps working and any enabled AC interrupt can wake the CPU. Single-shot comparisons in sleep start only from events. The AC also works while its clock is stopped, as long as it is powered. In continuous mode the comparator runs asynchronously and an edge matching the interrupt condition starts GCLK_AC_DIG to register it, waking the device if the interrupt is enabled; no filtering is possible this way. An event-triggered single-shot comparison in sleep can use the filter.

Bus and generic clocks are asynchronous: a synchronized access sets STATUS.SYNCBUSY until it completes, and an access needing synchronization while it is set stalls the bus. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, COMPCTRLn.ENABLE and WINCTRL.
The DAC is one 10-bit channel converting at up to 350 ksps, with several trigger sources, a high-drive output buffer, DMA support, and an output that can feed the analog comparator (and the ADC).

The DAC pins are set up through PORT. It runs in any sleep mode in which its clock runs and its interrupts can wake the device. CLK_DAC_APB is gated in the Power Manager; the generic clock GCLK_DAC must be enabled in GCLK first, and being asynchronous to the bus clock, some writes are synchronized. The DMA request needs the DMAC, the interrupt line the NVIC. The DAC keeps running when the CPU halts in debug. Every writable register except INTFLAG can be write-protected by the PAC, off during debug halt and never against an external debugger.

A value written to DATA is converted and appears at the output after the conversion time; events can trigger conversions instead. Choose the reference in CTRLB.REFSEL before enabling. CTRLA.ENABLE turns the DAC on; CTRLA.SWRST resets every register and disables it. CTRLB.EOEN enables the output driver onto VOUT, a high-drive buffer for resistive and capacitive loads; enable it only when the output is needed, to save power. The range runs from GND to the reference: the internal 1 V (INT1V, the default), the analog supply (AVCC = VDDANA) or VREFA. CTRLB.IOEN routes the output internally to the analog comparator, alone or together with the external output; to feed the ADC the output buffer must be on.

operation.topic: DAC data buffer, pump and sampling period
operation.text: DATABUF and DATA form a two-stage FIFO: the start-conversion event (EVCTRL.STARTEI) moves DATABUF into DATA and starts a conversion; an event while DATABUF is empty raises an underrun interrupt if enabled. When DATABUF empties, a data-buffer-empty event (EVCTRL.EMPTYEO) and interrupt can ask for new data. Below 2.5 V the voltage pump must run; it is switched on by itself as the supply requires, and CTRLB.VPD = 1 turns it off to save power above 2.5 V. The pump uses GCLK_DAC, which must run at least four times faster than the sampling rate. Nothing signals the end of a conversion, so the sampling period must be at least the specified conversion time.

The DMA request EMPTY is set when DATABUF has passed to DATA and cleared when DATABUF is written; since DATABUF starts full, the CPU must write it before the first event. CPU access to the registers that set or clear a DMA request can lose the request or corrupt the transfer. With the PAC protecting the DAC, DATABUF cannot be written unless CTRLB.BDWP = 1. Interrupt sources are data buffer empty, underrun and synchronization ready, on one common line; read INTFLAG to tell them apart. The output event is EMPTY (EVCTRL.xxEO) and the input event START (EVCTRL.xxEI), acted on for any connected event.

GCLK_DAC runs in idle sleep. In standby the output buffer keeps its value if CTRLA.RUNSTDBY = 1 and is disabled if it is zero. A synchronized access sets STATUS.SYNCBUSY until done (the SYNCRDY interrupt can mark it); one made while it is set stalls the bus. Synchronized on write: CTRLA.SWRST, CTRLA.ENABLE, DATA and DATABUF; on read: DATA.

The peripheral touch controller measures capacitive touch sensors: buttons, sliders, wheels and proximity sensing, in self-capacitance or mutual-capacitance mode, mixed freely. Self-capacitance uses one pin (a Y line) per sensor; mutual capacitance uses one pin per X line and one per Y line in an X-Y matrix, including ITO grids. Buttons: 7, 13 or 16 in self-capacitance and 12, 42 or 72 in mutual capacitance, for the 14-, 20- and 24-pin devices. It needs one pin per electrode and no external parts, compensates parasitic capacitance with adjustable gain, calibrates and recalibrates itself so readings do not drift with temperature or supply, measures single-shot or free-running, filters noise in hardware and de-synchronizes against conducted noise, has a selectable settling delay on a channel change, starts on a command or an event, and interrupts on completion: scanning 10 channels every 50 ms takes 5% of the CPU. It is configured through the QTouch Composer tool and driven by the QTouch Library linked into the application.

X and Y pins connect straight to the sensor electrodes; no external parts are needed, though a 1 kΩ series resistor on each X and Y line improves EMC. A mutual-capacitance sensor is the capacitance between an X electrode, which transmits, and a Y electrode, which receives; a self-capacitance sensor is one Y electrode whose own capacitance is measured. Inside, each Y line meets a series resistor RS and a 100 kΩ resistor ahead of the compensation circuit and the acquisition module (gain control, ADC, filtering), which gives a 10-bit result and an interrupt.

The PTC runs from GCLK_PTC, an asynchronous clock independent of the system and bus clocks, whose source is chosen in the generic clock controller and which must be enabled in the Power Manager (off by default). GCLK_PTC runs from 400 kHz to 4 MHz.
Typical values are at 25 °C unless stated; minimum and maximum values hold over the operating temperature and voltage ranges unless stated.

Current consumption is measured, except where noted, with VDDIN at 3.3 V (or 1.8 V with the CPU running from Flash with 3 wait states); XOSC stopped, XOSC32K running on an external 32 kHz crystal and DFLL48M locked to it at 48 MHz as the main clock; CPU and AHB clocks undivided, APBA divided by 4, APBB and APBC bridges off; only the NVMCTRL and APBA bridge AHB clocks and the PM, SYSCTRL and RTC peripheral clocks running; I/Os inactive with internal pull-up; CPU on Flash with 1 wait state; NVMCTRL cache on; BOD33 off. Wake-up time runs from the edge of the wake-up signal to the first instruction fetched from Flash. The current is measured with an ammeter (Amp 0) in the common supply feeding VDDIN, VDDANA and VDDIO.

Each peripheral's figure is Iperiph − Idefault. Idefault is taken with VDDIN at 3.3 V, XOSC stopped, XOSC32K on its 32 kHz crystal, OSC8M at 8 MHz as main clock, CPU, AHB and APBn clocks undivided, only the NVMCTRL and HPB0-2 bridge AHB clocks and the PM and SYSCTRL peripheral clocks running, I/Os inactive with pull-up, CPU in IDLE0, cache on and BOD33 off. Iperiph is taken with the peripheral's GCLK set up and enabled where relevant, its clock unmasked and the peripheral enabled, the CPU in IDLE0; the CPU is then woken through the EIC (asynchronous level detection, no filter) and the peripheral, its clock and its GCLK are turned off again.

USB figures are taken with VDDIN at 3.3 V; in device mode the DFLL48M runs in USB clock recovery mode without a crystal (in host mode closed-loop on XOSC32K with a 32 kHz crystal); CPU, AHB and APBn clocks undivided; only the NVMCTRL and HPB0-2 bridge AHB clocks running; I/Os inactive with pull-up; CPU in IDLE0; cache on; BOD33 off; a 1.5 m USB cable. They leave out the clock source and the CPU, though no CPU activity is needed in any state. In device mode they include up to 200 µA through the D+ pull-up used for attach, which depends on the host.
Used as ordinary I/Os, the XOSC and XOSC32 pins behave as normal I/O pins, and the external reset pin has the electrical characteristics of a normal I/O pin (normal I/O pins characteristics table).
The power-on reset holds the device in reset while VDD rises until it passes VPOT+, and asserts reset again when VDD falls below VPOT-.
With hysteresis off, BOD33 holds reset while VCC is below the single level VBOD. With hysteresis on, reset is asserted when VCC falls below VBOD- and released when it rises above VBOD+.

Seen from outside, an ADC input is a series resistance RSAMPLE into a sampling capacitor CSAMPLE (whose far side sits at VDDIN/2). The source, with its own resistance RSOURCE, must charge CSAMPLE within the sampling time for full accuracy, so RSOURCE enters the sample-and-hold time.

The sensor is linear but depends on the internal reference, which itself drifts with temperature. Each device carries a read-only Temperature Log row at 0x00806030, written in production test, from which software refines its readings. Its values were taken with VDDIN = VDDIO = VDDANA = 3.3 V, ADC clock 1.0 MHz, 125 ksps, 57 µs sampling time, free-running with 4-sample averaging, each value the mean of 10 conversions, INT1V (1.0 V) as reference and the temperature sensor as input. It holds the room and hot test temperatures (integer and decimal parts: ROOM_TEMP_VAL_INT = 25 with ROOM_TEMP_VAL_DEC = 2 means 25.2 °C), the 12-bit ADC result at each, and the INT1V value at each as a two's complement offset from 1 V in 1 mV steps: 0 to 127 means 1 V down to 0.873 V and −1 to −127 means 1.001 V to 1.127 V, so INT1V = 1 − VAL/1000 in both ranges.

PTC current grows with the number of sensors, with sample averaging and with faster scanning. At 10 ms scans and no averaging one sensor draws about 96 µA (frequency mode None, PTC clock 4 MHz), ten sensors about 530 µA and, at 50 ms scans, fifty sensors about 620 µA; at 200 ms scans one sensor draws about 11 µA. Scanning 10 channels every 50 ms takes about 5% of the CPU, 100 channels every 10 ms about 70%.

The USB buffers meet the USB 2.0 electrical specification, where their AC parameters are defined; the interface is USB-IF certified as low/full-speed peripheral silicon (TID 40001664). USB compliance needs a CPU clock above 8 MHz while USB is active (no limit in suspend), a supply of 3.3 V (3.0 V min, 3.6 V max), and in device mode a GCLK_USB of 48 MHz within ±0.25%.

In master mode the SPI timing is referred to SS, SCK (CPOL 0 or 1), MISO in and MOSI out: tMOS from SS to the first SCK edge, tSCK the period, tSCKW the high/low width, tSCKR/tSCKF the edges, tMIS/tMIH MISO setup and hold, tMOH MOSI hold. In slave mode: tSSS SS setup to SCK, tSSH SS hold, tSSCK, tSSCKW, tSSCKR, tSSCKF for SCK, tSIS/tSIH MOSI setup and hold, tSOSSS MISO valid after SS falls, tSOS MISO setup and tSOSSH MISO hold after SS rises.

The I2C timing is referred to SCL and SDA: tR rise and tOF fall times, tLOW and tHIGH the SCL low and high periods, tHD;STA hold after a (repeated) START, tSU;STA setup for a repeated START, tHD;DAT and tSU;DAT data hold and setup, tSU;STO setup for STOP and tBUF the bus free time between STOP and START.

In a read cycle the debugger drives stop, park and a turnaround on SWDIO, the device answers with the acknowledge, data and parity, then the line turns around again; in a write cycle the device gives the acknowledge and the debugger then drives data and parity. THIGH and TLOW are the SWDCLK high and low periods, TOS the skew of SWDIO output to the falling SWDCLK edge, TIS and TIH the SWDIO setup and hold around the rising SWDCLK edge.

In an electrically noisy environment, beyond normal EMC practice, three things matter most for reliable operation: decoupling capacitors right at the power pins, RC filtering of RESET, and SWCLK pulled up. Noise should also be kept from reaching the supply pins, the I/O pins and the crystals.
The decoupling below is needed only when an external analog reference is used; with the internal references it can be left off.

The reset circuit is needed only while the RESET function is in use, and its push-button only for a manual reset. RESET is enabled on its pin after power-up; it is released for GPIO use through the EXTCTRL register. The pin has an internal pull-up, so the external one is optional. The pull-up keeps RESET from falling by accident; the resistor in series with the switch discharges the filter capacitor gently, so pressing the switch does not cause a current surge and noise spike.

Unused pins left in their default state draw the least leakage, so they need no configuration to save power. The device can run from internal clocks, external clocks or a mix, for example the internal 8 MHz oscillator for the system clock and a 32.768 kHz watch crystal for the RTC.

The low-frequency oscillator is built for a 32.768 kHz watch crystal and for very low current, so the crystal's load capacitance and ESR (from its datasheet) need care; the 32 kHz crystal oscillator table gives the maximum ESR for 12.5 pF crystals. The oscillator's own internal load capacitance plus the board's can be enough for a crystal of less than 12.5 pF load capacitance with no external capacitors; the crystal's datasheet may call for external capacitors to improve accuracy and safety factor, and gives the load capacitance to aim for.

The crystal sees, on each side, the device's internal capacitance CLn (to ground inside the oscillator), the board's parasitic capacitance CELn and any external load capacitor CPn, all in parallel to ground. CELn is usually small enough to ignore; when it counts it depends on board material and layout. The total should equal the load capacitance in the crystal's datasheet. The internal pin capacitances are in the electrical characteristics.

Programming and debugging use the Serial Wire Debug interface, served by Atmel and third-party tools such as SAM-ICE, JTAGICE3 or the embedded debugger of the Xplained Pro kit, which needs no external debugger. A pull-up on SWCLK is critical for reliable operation.
JTAGICE3 does not take the Cortex 10-pin connector directly: either its squid cable is wired to the signals by hand, or a 10-pin header with the JTAGICE3 pinout lets its cable plug straight in.

The USB interface is the D+/D- pair plus VBUS and GND; the operating voltages that allow USB are in the electrical characteristics. Match the pair's impedance on the board, route both lines alike (length, width, vias) and side by side with few bends and vias. Dedicated transient suppressors on D+, D- and VBUS, close to the connector, raise ESD protection. Tying the cable shield straight to the ground plane would make the cable an antenna, so shield and ground are joined through an RC filter.
Revision A was not sampled.
Revision B: the MBIST pause-on-error option does not work. Workaround: do not use it.
Revision B: two writes to CRCDATAIN in consecutive instructions can give a wrong CRC. Workaround: put a NOP between writes to CRCDATAIN.
Revision B: NVM CTRLB.MANW resets to 0, so a data write through a stray pointer into the NVM range can write the NVM. Workaround: set CTRLB.MANW to 1 at start-up.
Revision B: while external reset is held, VDDIO leakage is high. Workaround: keep external reset active as briefly as possible.

Revision B: on some parts BOD12 is re-enabled too early when leaving standby, which can reset the device with BOD12 as the cause. Workaround: just before entering standby write 0x00000004 to address 0x40000838 to disable BOD12, and write 0x00000006 there on wake-up to re-enable it.

Revision B: the SYSTICK calibration value is wrong; the right value is 0x40000000. It should not be used to load the SysTick reload register, which is set from the main clock frequency and the wanted tick period (the Arm Cortex-M0+ documentation describes SysTick).

operation.topic: Erratum 10416: read-synchronized registers with APB clock stopped
operation.text: Revision B: reading a read-synchronized register while its APB clock is stopped and its GCLK runs freezes the system: CPU and DAP AHB-AP stall and debugging becomes impossible. Workaround: avoid such reads; recover by power cycling or a reset through the RESETN pin.
Revision B: the voltage regulator's low-power mode does not work above 85 °C. Workaround: keep the regulator in normal mode in standby by setting SYSCTRL VREG.RUNSTDBY = 1.

operation.topic: Erratum 13574: I2C slave CTRLB writes in interrupts
operation.text: Revision B: in I2C slave mode, writing CTRLB inside the AMATCH or DRDY interrupt handlers can reset the state machine. Workaround: to set CTRLB.ACKACT to 0, write STATUS = 0 and then CTRLB = 0; to set it to 1, write STATUS = 0 and then CTRLB = SERCOM_I2CS_CTRLB_ACKACT; make each pair atomic by masking higher-priority interrupts, and use these writes in place of read-modify-write of ACKACT. Otherwise write CTRLB in those handlers only to end a transaction. When not ending a transaction, clear AMATCH by writing 1 to its flag instead of using CTRLB.CMD; DRDY clears itself on a DATA access in smart mode, otherwise by writing 1 to its flag. In place of CTRLB.CMD = 0x3 to acknowledge an address, clear PREC if it is set (CMD 0x3 clears every flag) and then clear AMATCH by writing its flag.

operation.topic: Erratum 12164: GCLK generators on a failed XOSC32K
operation.text: Revision B: if the external XOSC32K fails, neither the RST pin nor a GCLK software reset resets the generators clocked from it. Workaround: power cycle the device to reset them.
Revision B: writing a DFLL register before the DFLL clock is requested can freeze the device. Workaround: clear DFLLCTRL.ONDEMAND before configuring the DFLL.

operation.topic: Erratum 11938: DFLL status after USB suspend
operation.text: Revision B: in USB clock recovery mode the DFLL status bits in PCLKSR can be wrong after a USB suspend. Workaround: do not watch those bits in USB recovery mode.

Revision B: reaching the minimum or maximum COARSE or FINE value while locking raises an out-of-bounds interrupt even if the final lock values are within range. Workaround: enable the DFLLOOB interrupt only after both DFLLLCKC and DFLLLCKF are set in SYSCTRL INTFLAG.

operation.topic: Erratum 15341: EIC spurious flag on enable
operation.text: Revision B: with an EIC line set to low level, rising edge or both edges and its filter on, a false INTFLAG.EXTINT[x] can appear when the EIC is enabled. Workaround: clear the flag after enabling the EIC and before enabling its interrupts.

operation.topic: Erratum 12003: I2C SCL low extend time-outs
operation.text: Revision B: the slave and master SCL low extend time-outs (CTRLA.SEXTTOEN, CTRLA.MEXTTOEN) do not work with the SCL low time-out (CTRLA.LOWTOUT) off, because GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW is then not requested. Workaround: set CTRLA.LOWTOUT = 1 to use them.
Revision B: in USART auto-baud mode a missing stop bit is not flagged as an inconsistent sync (ISF) or framing (FERR) error. No workaround.
Revision B: enabling the SERCOM in SPI mode with CTRLB.SSDE and CTRLB.RXEN both set can raise a false INTFLAG.SSL. Workaround: enable it with RXEN = 0 and set RXEN = 1 in a later write.

operation.topic: Erratum 12499: I2C master in debug halt
operation.text: Revision B: with DBGCTRL.DBGSTOP set, an I2C master transaction does not stop at once when the CPU halts in debug; it stops after the current byte, raising its interrupt if enabled. Workaround: keep DBGCTRL.DBGSTOP = 0 in I2C master mode while debugging.

operation.topic: Erratum 14817: TCC advanced capture channel order
operation.text: Revision B: the advanced capture modes (CAPTMIN, CAPTMAX, LOCMIN, LOCMAX, DERIV0) fail unless every higher channel also uses one of them; for example CC[0] = CAPTMIN and CC[1] = CAPTMAX with CC[2] and CC[3] = CAPTEN does not work. Workaround: put basic capture on the lower channels and advanced capture on the upper ones, as CC[0] = CC[1] = CAPTEN, CC[2] = CAPTMIN, CC[3] = CAPTMAX.

Revision B: in RAMP2 mode with a fault set to keep, qualified and restart, a fault at the end of the period in the qualified state can restart the next ramp twice. Workaround: avoid faults in the few cycles around the end or start of a ramp.
Revision B: not every DMA MCx trigger is raised on a CCx match. Workaround: update CC and CCBUF through DMA on the OVF trigger.

operation.topic: Erratum 12519: TCC blanking on first increment
operation.text: Revision B: with blanking on, a recoverable fault arriving while a counting-up TCC makes its first step is not blanked. No workaround.

operation.topic: Erratum 12354: TCC retrigger in dual-slope mode
operation.text: Revision B: in dual-slope mode the counter is left uncleared by a retrigger event. No workaround.
Revision B: in two-ramp mode an event comes at the end of each ramp, two per cycle, so EVCTRL.CNTSEL.END cannot mark the end of the double-ramp cycle. No workaround.

operation.topic: Erratum 12477: TCC RUNSTDBY written while enabled
operation.text: Revision B: writing RUNSTDBY after the TCC is enabled stalls that TCC's APB bus, and CTRLA.RUNSTDBY is not enable-protected. No workaround.
Revision B: fault filtering does not work on an inverted fault input. Workaround: use non-inverted faults only.

This set of figures covers operation up to 105 °C ambient. Typical values are at 25 °C unless stated; minimum and maximum values hold over the whole operating temperature and voltage range unless stated.

The current figures are measured with VDDIN at 3.3 V (or 1.8 V where stated, the CPU then running from Flash with 3 wait states); XOSC stopped; XOSC32K running on an external 32 kHz crystal; DFLL48M at 48 MHz referenced to XOSC32K and used as main clock unless stated; CPU and AHB clocks undivided, APBA divided by 4, the APBB and APBC bridges off; only the NVMCTRL and APBA bridge AHB clocks and the PM, SYSCTRL and RTC peripheral clocks running; I/Os inactive with internal pull-up; CPU on Flash with 1 wait state; NVMCTRL cache on; BOD33 off. Wake-up time runs from the edge of the wake-up signal to the first instruction fetched from Flash.
The supply current is measured with one ammeter (Amp 0) in the common supply that feeds VDDIN, VDDANA and VDDIO. The USB peripheral's own consumption is given separately.

USB figures are taken with VDDIN at 3.3 V; in device mode the DFLL48M runs in USB clock recovery mode without a crystal, in host mode closed-loop on XOSC32K with a 32 kHz crystal; CPU, AHB and APBn clocks undivided; only the NVMCTRL and HPB0-2 bridge AHB clocks running; I/Os inactive with pull-up; CPU in IDLE0; cache on; BOD33 off; a 1.5 m USB cable; the device and host states run as the USB 2.0 standard defines them. The figures leave out the clock source and the CPU, though no CPU activity is needed in any state. In device mode they include up to 200 µA through the D+ pull-up used for attach, a figure that depends on the host.
Reset is held while VDD rises until it passes VPOT+, and asserted again once VDD falls below VPOT-.
With hysteresis off, BOD33 holds reset while VCC is below the single level VBOD. With hysteresis on, reset is asserted when VCC falls below VBOD- and released when it rises above VBOD+.
The ADC can average a number of consecutive conversions in hardware to gain accuracy; AVGCTRL.SAMPLENUM[3:0] sets how many, and the mean lands in RESULT.

operation.topic: ADC offset and gain correction at 105 °C
operation.text: Offset and gain errors limit absolute accuracy; the values in OFFSETCORR and GAINCORR are applied to each conversion before it is written to RESULT.

operation.topic: ADC input and sample-and-hold time at 105 °C
operation.text: Seen from outside, an ADC input is a series resistance RSAMPLE into a sampling capacitor CSAMPLE. The source, with its own resistance RSOURCE, has to charge CSAMPLE within the sampling time for full accuracy, so RSOURCE enters the required sample-and-hold time.

The sensor is linear, but its reading depends on the internal reference, which itself drifts with temperature. Each device holds a read-only Temperature Log row at 0x00806030, written in production test, from which software refines its readings. Its values were taken with VDDIN = VDDIO = VDDANA = 3.3 V, ADC clock 1.0 MHz, 125 ksps, 57 µs sampling time, free-running with 4-sample averaging, each value the mean of 10 conversions, INT1V (1.0 V) as reference and the temperature sensor as input. It holds the room and hot test temperatures (integer and decimal parts: ROOM_TEMP_VAL_INT = 25 with ROOM_TEMP_VAL_DEC = 2 is 25.2 °C), the 12-bit ADC result at each, and the INT1V value at each as a two's complement offset from 1 V in 1 mV steps: 0 to 127 is 1 V down to 0.873 V and −1 to −127 is 1.001 V to 1.127 V, so INT1V = 1 − VAL/1000 in both ranges.

The crystal sits between Xin and Xout with one capacitor CLEXT from each pin to ground. The crystal is modelled as a series LM, RM and CM branch in parallel with its shunt capacitance CSHUNT; CSTRAY is the stray capacitance of the pins and board. The same connection and load-capacitor relation apply to the 32 kHz oscillator.

PTC current rises with the number of sensors and with sample averaging, and is highest on the 10 ms series and lowest on the 200 ms series. With no averaging, frequency mode None and a 4 MHz PTC clock, one sensor draws about 96 µA on the 10 ms series and about 11 µA on the 200 ms series; ten sensors about 528 µA on the 10 ms series; fifty sensors about 620 µA on the 50 ms series. CPU utilization at the graph's first point, 10, is about 20 % for 1 channel, 25 % for 10 channels and 70 % for 100 channels, and it is a few percent at 100 and 200.

The USB buffers meet the USB 2.0 electrical specification, which holds their AC parameters; the interface is USB-IF certified as low/full-speed peripheral silicon (TID 40001664). USB compliance needs a CPU clock above 8 MHz while USB is active (no limit in suspend), a supply of 3.3 V (3.0 V min, 3.6 V max), and in device mode a GCLK_USB of 48 MHz within ±0.25%.

In master mode the SPI timing is referred to SS, SCK (CPOL 0 or 1), MISO in and MOSI out: tMOS MOSI setup to SCK, tSCK the period, tSCKW the high and low width, tSCKR and tSCKF the edges, tMIS and tMIH MISO setup and hold, tMOH MOSI hold. In slave mode: tSSS SS setup to SCK, tSSH SS hold, tSSCK, tSSCKW, tSSCKR and tSSCKF for SCK, tSIS and tSIH MOSI setup and hold, tSOSSS MISO valid after SS falls, tSOS MISO setup and tSOSSH MISO hold after SS rises.

The I2C timing is referred to SCL and SDA: tR rise and tOF fall times, tLOW and tHIGH the SCL low and high periods, tHD;STA hold after a (repeated) START, tSU;STA setup for a repeated START, tHD;DAT and tSU;DAT data hold and setup, tSU;STO setup for STOP and tBUF the bus free time between STOP and START.
